Chapter 2

From Fintech to Green Fintech:

How to Decarbonize the AI in the Financial Domain

Roberto Vergallo

https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3560-806X

Pegaso University, Italy

Simone Casciaro

https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9194-4853

Salento University, Italy

Luca Mainetti

https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9387-9277

Salento University, Italy

ABSTRACT

Machine Learning and Deep Learning are spreading at incredible pace in finance. However, the related energy consumption lacks in coherence with the sustainability requirements of banks and financial institutions. Particularly, as the energy required to run complex algorithms increases, more CO2 is released because of the power grid relying mostly on fossil fuels. While techniques are arising to mitigate the carbon footprint of AI, Fintech is facing the challenge of integrating such strategies within the peculiarities of the domain, which requires timeliness, data protection and compliance. In this work, we present the state-of-the-art Green AI techniques, reporting the available experimental results, and critically evaluating their applicability in the financial domain. This contribution is useful for financial institutions, Fintech startups and regulatory bodies who wants to measure and mitigate the impact of AI in the field, decarbonize old or new AI-based products and services, and assess the effectiveness of decarbonization efforts.

1. INTRODUCTION

2023 was the year of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The introduction of ChatGPT by OpenAI on the market has marked a significative breakpoint in our recent history, having a deep impact on the technological development and setting the foundations of a new AI-aided society. This incredible breakdown has been possible thanks to the big advancements in the complexity and performance increase of Large Language Models (LLM), which motivated all the ICT companies to stay up to date with the AI revolution in order to meet user’s expectations in our fast-moving society.

The financial sector is not exempt from the impacts of this significative breakpoint in human history. While the implementation of AI techniques within banking processes is undergoing from long time – whether the customer aware or not of it – the race towards the implementation of intelligent systems, able to fast automate the execution of tasks traditionally executed by humans, has now reached momentum. This has pushed regulatory bodies such as central banks and national banks to issue specific regulations to harmonize the development of AI in finance with the final aim of protecting the customer. In fact, issues like privacy management, explainability of decisions, fair competition, and technological sustainability are point of attentions for regulatory bodies who must ensure that all the new AI-based product and services would not harm or offend the banking customers, which have the right not to be discriminated nor violated in their fundamental rights.

Particularly, the sustainability aspect is not entirely new in banking. The responsibilities in the matters of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) sustainability make banks and financial institutions under strict surveillance, being themselves obliged to prove their factual commitment in measuring and mitigating their non-economic impact on people and the environment. AI has proven to have a remarkable power consumption, because of the complexity of their algorithms which require a significative amount of processing resources and times. Recent research of the International Energy Agency shown that electricity consumption from data centers, AI and the cryptocurrency sector could double by 20261. Indeed, after globally consuming an estimated 460 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2022, data centers’ total electricity consumption could reach more than 1 000 TWh in 2026. These data agree with previous research of 2018 when Belkhir & Elmeligi (2018) showed that the whole Information and Communication Technology (ICT) sector will reach 14% of global carbon footprint estimated for 2040, comparable to the entire aviation industry. Even the use of generative AI, like ChatGPT, contributes to this impact. A single query generates approximately 4.32g of CO2, and 15 queries equal the emissions of one hour of video streaming on Netflix. Beyond energy, water consumption is also significant: generating 100 words with ChatGPT consumes the equivalent of a bottle of water, and Google Gemini’s data centers consume nearly a quarter of the water needed for a city the size of Dallas.

These forecasts represent quite a big problem for the Fintech field, given both the sustainability requirements and its needs in computational resources, i.e. energy. The more energy it uses, the more fossil fuels are burnt to meet the exponential demands. A shift from Fintech to Green Fintech is needed to decarbonize this industry. How to make banks able to meet ESG criteria if AI is so avid in resources? A risk the financial sector is facing is the unsustainability of its recent progress towards AI. Since it can be assumed there is no way back to a world without AI, the research should give the financial domains all the conceptual, methodological and technical tools needed to measure and mitigate the impact of the AI it is using.

Software sustainability is emerging as a fundamental metric of quality and innovation, alongside traditional measures like maintainability, efficiency, and code security. In software quality assurance (QA), the industry is accustomed to considering metrics such as bug count, execution speed, test coverage, and robustness. However, a broader perspective is needed: the planet as a stakeholder. Software is not merely a product or tool; it is also a significant consumer of energy and water resources. Incorporating environmental impact as a quality metric is critical to ensuring that technological advances do not compromise the future of the planet. In the last two years, a new discipline called Green Software Engineering (GSE), or Sustainable Software Engineering (SSE), has emerged. GSE has many definitions, one of them is the following: GSE is the discipline that studies the process of creating software systems that are able to create value in the long term without hindering its surrounding environment. As also worded by Microsoft’s former developer A. Hussain2, now Executive Director at the Green Software Foundation3, a carbon-efficient application is one that extracts the maximum value for each gram of carbon it is responsible for emitting into the atmosphere. In addition to traditional metrics such as technical debt or scalability, sustainability can be viewed as a parallel dimension of quality. Integrating sustainability into software quality practices is not only an ethical choice but also a strategic one. The planet, as a stakeholder, demands that companies consider their environmental impact. Investing in sustainable software leads to improved overall quality, reduced energy costs, enhanced corporate reputation, and a competitive edge. By adopting sustainability as a quality metric, companies can act responsibly today to build a safer, more prosperous future for businesses, users, and the planet.

Currently, the research in the topic of GSE is mainly empirical, because the effectiveness of the emerging carbon mitigation techniques is still unknown. Particularly, the Green AI subfield investigates the effectiveness of techniques and tools able to mitigate the energy consumption and carbon emissions of AI on the entire pipeline, with special attention on three phases: development (training), production (inference), and maintenance (update of the models, i.e. re-training). Some of these techniques involve the workload relocation in space and time, according to the high variability of renewables in the energy mix.

While the aforementioned techniques – which will be adequately described in this chapter – are providing interesting results in general, some issues arise because of the specificity of the financial fields. Particularly, the mandatory adherence to regulations, and the strict timing requirement of financial use cases make such techniques not immediately applicable to AI in Fintech. Moreover, being the current literature in the field of Green AI very fragmented, it is not easy for Fintech practitioners, regulators, companies/startups, and researchers to grasp an overall view of both the available strategies and the challenges given by the constraints and limitations of the field. Therefore, the main objective of this chapter is to serve as a “one stop-shop” for the aforementioned stakeholders who are interested in decarbonizing the AI in financial applications. This chapter delves into several crucial topics that are central to advancing sustainability in the Fintech sector. It begins by examining carbon metrics, which are essential for measuring the environmental impact of Fintech operations and guiding efforts toward decarbonization. We then explore the fundamental principles of green software design, emphasizing the need for sustainable coding practices and energy-efficient software architecture. The chapter also reviews ongoing standardization initiatives that aim to establish common frameworks and guidelines for integrating sustainability into the Fintech ecosystem. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the state of the art in both green Fintech and green AI, highlighting the latest developments and the growing interest in leveraging AI technologies to promote sustainability within the financial industry. Case studies are presented to showcase how AI is already being applied in Fintech to drive more sustainable practices and to understand the challenges faced in the industry. A key focus of the chapter is on the techniques used to decarbonize the two main stages of AI in Fintech: the training step and the deployment step. We analyze strategies for reducing the energy consumption and carbon footprint associated with both, offering insights into how these techniques can be implemented effectively within the financial sector. Throughout the discussion, we emphasize the regulatory implications and other domain-specific requirements that influence the adoption of these decarbonization strategies.

The rest of the chapter is structured as follows. The first section reports the technical background with a focus on sustainability standards. The second section depicts the literature review in the domains of green Fintech and Green AI, also evidencing open issues and motivations. The third and fourth sections specifically describes the techniques of carbon-aware AI suitable for the financial domain: the former related to the training phase, the latter on the deployment phase. The fifth section carries out a careful discussion. The sixth and last section summarizes the results, including the final remarks.

2. TECHNICAL BACKGROUND AND STANDARDIZATION INITIATIVES

Carbon Intensity Metrics

Renewable energy is becoming increasingly dominant due to its cost advantages over traditional energy sources and its continued decrease in cost as technology advances. To accelerate the transition to renewable energy, it is essential to enhance the financial attractiveness of renewable projects while reducing the profitability of fossil fuel-based energy production. An effective strategy involves increasing electricity usage when it is generated by low-carbon sources, such as wind and solar, and reducing usage when high-carbon sources, like coal and natural gas, are supplying power.

Being “carbon-aware” entails adjusting energy consumption based on the Carbon Intensity of the power grid at any given time. Carbon Intensity encompasses a range of metrics that assess the environmental impact of energy production in specific times and locations. Given that the energy consumed is a mix of fossil and renewable sources, the impact of producing a unit of energy can vary significantly across time and regions. While abundant energy is available, efficient capture and storage remain challenges.

The deployment of renewables is expanding globally, influenced by the availability of natural resources in different regions. However, renewables like solar and wind energy are intermittent; sunlight, wind patterns, and cloud coverage are beyond direct human control. Additionally, political decisions play a significant role in the level of investment in renewables. This is especially relevant for certain clean energy sources, such as nuclear power, which – despite its low emissions – raises unique concerns regarding perceived risks. Due to these factors, increased energy demand or decreased renewable availability often necessitates reliance on fossil fuels, thereby raising the Carbon Intensity. Measuring the current “dirtiness” of energy in use at any specific moment allows for informed decisions on the optimal timing and location for energy consumption.

Carbon Intensity is measured in mass per unit of energy (typically kg/kWh or lbs/kWh). The mass refers to the quantity of CO2eq. The CO2 equivalent unit of measure is preferred to the simple CO2 because there are several Green House Gases (GHG) that can be harmful for the atmosphere, each with different impacts on global warming. The Kyoto Protocol, signed in 1997, defined 7 harmful GHG, of which Carbon Dioxide is the less harmful. Other GHG includes Methane (CH4), Nitrous Oxide (N2O), Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), Perfluorocarbons (PFCs), Sulphur Hexafluoride (SF6), and Nitrogen Trifluoride (NF3). GHG emissions by human activities are the main root of the Global Warming. Since it is impractical, and even meaningless, to have 7 different Carbon Intensity signals, emissions are converted to their carbon dioxide equivalent. Even if a system is not directly emitting carbon dioxide, it remains essential to measure its carbon impact.

Another important consideration is that not all greenhouse gases impact the environment over the same time span. By convention, the environmental impact is typically calculated based on gases with a 100-year impact, referred to as the 100-year Global Warming Potential (100-GWP). The following table is computed using this standard.

Table 1. The 100-GWP values for some of the green house gases defined in the Kyoto protocol

GHG

100-GWP

Carbon dioxide

1

Methane

21

Nitrous oxide

310

Sulphur hexafluoride

23,900

According to the previous table, 1kg of Methane (CH4) is estimated to be 21 times

more harmful than 1kg of Carbon Dioxide (CO2). A weight function is defined to combine all gas emissions into their carbon dioxide equivalent:

  • Equation 1. Carbon Dioxide Equivalent Weight Function

${CO}_{2}eq = {\sum\limits_{g \in GHG}\left( {{GWP}_{g} \bullet m_{g}} \right)}$

Unfortunately, there is no reliable source of GWP: every single research work has its own calculations. They mostly agree with the overall magnitude of values, but actually they slight differs when providing precise numbers. The values presented in Table 1 are taken from Foster et al. (2007).

Two Carbon Intensity signals exists, and can be useful for different purposes. The simpler is the Average Operating Emissions Rate (AOER). AOER represents the average emissions rate of all electricity produced on the local grid at a given time. It is determined by adding up the total emissions from all generators within a specific hour and grid region, then dividing that by the total amount of energy produced. In general, average emissions are used to distribute responsibility for emissions evenly, rather than based on direct causation.

Suppose a scenario in which an operation is initially powered entirely by clean energy. If a new task is added, it may necessitate the activation of a coal-based power plant due to insufficient renewable energy to meet the increased demand. As a result, additional carbon emissions are generated. When calculating the average carbon emissions, these emissions are distributed across all tasks, even those originally powered by clean energy, simply because a single additional task required fossil fuel support. The Marginal Operating Emissions Rate (MOER) reflects the emissions rate of the electricity generator(s) that adjust in response to load fluctuations on the local grid at a given time (Figure 1). The MOER can effectively guide decisions to minimize emissions. IoT companies incorporate MOER forecasts into their device scheduling optimization or use them to create a UI feature that advises users on the best times to run appliances or charge an EV. Renewable energy buyers use historical MOER data to choose projects that reduce more emissions. In emissions accounting, MOER is used to calculate the emissions avoided by a project. MOER accounts for the impacts of renewable curtailment as well as the import and export of electricity between different grid regions.

Figure 1. Marginal Operating Emission Rate (MOER) principle

In the previous figure, the marginal cost and capacity in megawatts are shown for various energy sources. Coal is the least favorable due to its high marginal cost, while the sequence begins with renewables. When the capacity of renewable sources is exhausted, the system shifts to nuclear energy, and so forth. To train an AI model, it becomes necessary to increase demand from the current level to a higher demand point. In this context, rather than considering the overall Carbon Intensity of the data center, it is more relevant to calculate the marginal cost of moving from one demand level to another. By foregoing this task, the system would effectively reduce Carbon Intensity, which is why this measurement is referred to as marginal Carbon Intensity. This increase in demand, even for renewable-powered tasks, raises the overall carbon intensity of operations as additional energy sources are brought online.

There are a few web-based services able to provide real-time Carbon Intensity signals (both AOER and MOER). They are Electricity Maps4, WattTime5 and Carbon Aware SDK6. They all provide APIs than can be integrated with existing software. They also provide historical dataset and forecasts. Electricity Maps provides only AOER, while WattTime provides both AOER and MOER. The Carbon Aware SDK is a wrapper for the previous two providers, and it is maintained by the Green Software Foundation. WattTime also provides a health signal (only for the US territory), measured in cost per MWh. It is based on the principle of VSL (Value of Statistical Life), by which the value of a human life is valued as the price a person would pay to avoid the risk of a fatality. VSL in the US is 7.5M$7. The health signal measures the health damage (in dollar) caused by the generation of 1MWh (because of polluting the air).

Two carbon-aware techniques exist to mitigate the environmental footprint of software systems: demand shifting and demand shaping. They both use the Carbon Intensity metrics to change the behavior of software. They are described in the next two subsections.

Demand shifting. When activities, such as data-intensive tasks, allow for flexibility in timing or location, energy consumption can be optimized by selecting periods when the grid’s carbon footprint is lower. For instance, tasks like training a ML model can be postponed or relocated to times or places with a higher proportion of renewable energy. Research has shown that by adopting these practices, it’s possible to achieve significant carbon reductions, ranging from 45% to as much as 99% (Kelly et al. 2011), depending on the renewable energy mix available on the grid. Demand shifting can be categorized into two types: spatial shifting, which refers to adjusting energy use based on location, and temporal shifting, which involves altering energy consumption based on time. These strategies, when implemented, play a key role in maximizing renewable energy use and minimizing carbon emissions.

Spatial shifting refers to relocating computational tasks to a physical location where the Carbon Intensity of the energy supply is currently lower. This approach takes advantage of regions that rely more heavily on cleaner energy sources. For example, computation could be shifted between hemispheres based on seasonal variations in sunlight hours, maximizing the use of solar energy during periods of greater availability.

In cases where spatial shifting is not feasible, temporal shifting offers an alternative. This involves rescheduling computational tasks to times when Carbon Intensity is lower, such as during periods of increased solar or wind energy generation, which may occur later in the day or at night. Advances in weather forecasting allow for reasonably accurate predictions of future Carbon Intensity, enabling more informed decisions about when to perform energy-intensive operations.

Major technology companies have recognized the value of carbon-aware practices and are leveraging sophisticated modelling techniques to implement demand-shifting strategies. For instance, Google has developed Carbon-Aware Data Centres (Radovanović et al., 2022), a project aimed at aligning cloud workloads with periods of lower Carbon Intensity. Using predictive models to forecast both future Carbon Intensity and workload demand, Google optimizes the timing and location of large-scale tasks, ensuring that energy consumption coincides with periods of reduced carbon impact, without compromising system performance. Similarly, Microsoft has introduced a carbon-aware initiative in Windows 118, beginning with the scheduling of system updates during times of lower Carbon Intensity. This initiative aims to reduce the environmental footprint of routine computing operations by synchronizing them with cleaner energy availability. These examples highlight the increasing adoption of carbon-aware strategies, demonstrating how spatial and temporal demand shifting can contribute to reducing carbon emissions in the digital sector.

Demand shaping. It is a complementary strategy to demand shifting. Rather than relocating or rescheduling computational tasks, demand shaping involves adjusting the level of computational activity to align with the current energy supply. When the Carbon Intensity of the power grid is low, computational demand can be increased, allowing for more intensive tasks to be executed. Conversely, when Carbon Intensity is high, demand is reduced, resulting in fewer or less resource-intensive operations. In carbon-aware applications, demand shaping focuses on dynamically adjusting computational demands to match the fluctuating carbon costs of energy production. This process can be automated or left to the discretion of the user. For instance, eco modes – common in household appliances like cars or washing machines –represent a form of demand shaping. When eco mode is enabled, performance is deliberately reduced to conserve energy, offering users a choice between optimal performance and reduced resource consumption. Software applications can similarly incorporate eco modes, either automatically or through user consent, to minimize carbon emissions. A pertinent example is video conferencing software that automatically reduces video quality when bandwidth is low, prioritizing audio to maintain communication while consuming fewer resources. Another example can be seen in the TCP/IP protocol, where transfer speeds dynamically adjust based on network conditions and data volume. Web technologies also employ progressive enhancement, which improves the user experience based on the available bandwidth and device resources. Demand shaping strategy becomes particularly relevant when Carbon Intensity is high, where reducing demands or even cancelling processes altogether may be more effective than merely shifting tasks to another time or location. In the context of green software development, practitioners might opt to cancel or scale back processes during periods of high Carbon Intensity. By doing so, they reduce not only the energy demands of their applications but also help set more realistic expectations for end users, promoting a culture of sustainability in both software design and consumption.

Sustainable Web

As the Internet becomes an increasingly integral part of our daily lives, its environmental impact has grown significantly. The energy demands of data centers, server infrastructures, and large-scale web applications contribute to the digital sector’s rising carbon footprint. To combat this, the principles of sustainable web development has become vital. These approaches aim not only to improve the performance and user experience of websites but also to reduce their environmental impact by making web experiences more energy-efficient and eco-conscious.

Beyond traditional QA practices like test automation and bug management, several specific strategies directly contribute to sustainability. Performance budgeting, as detailed in the W3C’s Web Sustainability Guidelines9, is a central tool for ensuring that less energy is consumed as a result of lower data transfer and reduced page complexity. Performance budgeting involves setting limits on the amount of resources each page or feature is allowed to consume. This approach originates from the broader field of performance optimization, where developers aim to improve website speed and responsiveness. In performance budgeting, specific metrics – such as page weight, loading time, and the number of requests – are defined early in the development process, guiding design and technical choices to stay within these limits. For example, a performance budget might restrict the total size of images, scripts, or fonts that can be loaded on a single page. By enforcing these constraints, developers avoid unnecessary bloat, reduce bandwidth usage, and limit data transfer, which collectively lead to faster load times and a smoother user experience. Importantly, this practice also minimizes energy consumption across user devices and servers, since lower data loads require less processing power and fewer server resources. This leads to improvements in both software performance and environmental impact.

Additionally, a well-established practice in QA is the elimination of dead code or obsolete features to enhance maintainability. Removing unnecessary elements reduces the server workload and energy usage, showing how sustainability and code quality can converge to benefit both the software and the environment. Another impactful approach involves reducing the brightness of web pages. Lowering the average luminance of web interfaces can conserve battery life on user devices and reduce overall energy consumption, as highlighted by the W3C’s Susty Web group10. Furthermore, eliminating outdated or unused features not only streamlines the code but also reduces technical debt, enhancing maintainability while lowering energy demand.

To effectively measure and reduce a website’s environmental footprint, tools like CO2.js, developed by the Green Web Foundation11, offer valuable insights. This JavaScript library allows developers to estimate the CO2 emissions of a webpage based on its data transfer size. By using CO2.js, development teams can identify areas for optimization, helping reduce data transmission and energy consumption. The library’s comprehensive documentation is available on GitHub12, offering developers tangible metrics to work with as they aim to decrease the environmental impact of their digital products.

The Technology Carbon Standard13 by ScottLogic provides another useful framework for analyzing and mitigating IT emissions. It divides emissions into three stages: upstream, focusing on resource use during development (such as shutting down test servers overnight); operations, targeting reductions in emissions from on-premises data centers and advocating for cloud providers with greener energy sources; and downstream, which emphasizes optimizing software to lower energy consumption on end-user devices.

Sustainability principles for the web, as promoted by the W3C’s Sustainable Web Design Community Group (SustyWeb), further reinforce the importance of efficiency, longevity, and clean energy. Creating efficient web experiences by optimizing code and reducing page weight ensures that websites demand fewer resources. Designing for longevity reduces the need for frequent updates or complete rebuilds, saving both energy and developer resources. Furthermore, adopting renewable energy for hosting services can substantially cut the carbon footprint of websites and web applications.

For organizations seeking to integrate sustainability into their digital operations, a five-step action plan can serve as a roadmap. First, it’s essential to analyze emissions using tools like CO2.js to identify where the most significant environmental impacts occur. Next, clear sustainability goals should be defined, such as setting a maturity level for both the code and infrastructure, and incorporating sustainability into corporate KPIs. Third, eliminating unnecessary code and features will streamline the software and reduce energy consumption. The fourth step involves experimentation and innovation, encouraging the adoption of new, sustainable solutions with measurable goals. Finally, communication is critical: sharing sustainability initiatives with colleagues and users fosters greater engagement and commitment to reducing the environmental impact of digital services. By adopting these practices, companies can not only enhance the quality and efficiency of their software but also contribute to a more sustainable digital future, ensuring tangible benefits for users, stakeholders, and the planet.

For further details on how to implement these strategies, the whitepaper from the Climate Product Leaders group14 is a valuable resource.

Global Standardization Initiatives

Various organizations such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) have moved to promote regulations, standards, methodologies and guidelines to be able to promote the adoption and ethical, sustainable and transparent development of new technologies. A company that wants to use AI to offer new services in an environmentally sustainable way as well must abide by these regulations. Below we briefly present the main standards currently in place.

  • • Artificial Intelligence European Act15: AI systems can be a threat to the safety because can influence human decision-making, opinions, and actions. In 2021 a European commission proposed a set of rules designed to ensure the safety and fundamental rights of individuals and businesses who use AI systems in their daily activities and services. The committee ranks AI systems based on risk: unacceptable risk, high risk, limited risk and minimal risk. All EU member states must comply with this regulation and limit the security risks introduced with AI.

  • • ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management Systems16: It is an international standard that specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS) within organizations. For organizations, it sets out a structured way to manage risks and opportunities associated with AI, balancing innovation with governance.

  • • ISO/IEC 21031:2024 Software Carbon Intensity Specification17: This document describes a methodology for calculating the carbon emission rate of a software system using SCI score (Software Carbon Intensity score). Its purpose is to increase awareness of the environmental impact of the full stack of software infrastructure (hardware, software, network interfaces and so on) by providing a transparent, standardized method for assessing emissions. The key values for calculating the SCI score (Equation 2) are Operational Emissions (carbon emissions from the running of software), Embodied Emissions (carbon emissions from the physical resources required to run the software) and Function Unit (e.g. per user, per API calls etc.).

    • Equation 2.SCI Rate Equation

$SCI = \frac{\left( {~Operational~Emissions + Embodied~Emissions} \right)}{Function~Unit}$

  • • Operational emissions refer to the GHG produced during the active use of a system or device, including energy consumed while running software or powering hardware over time. Embodied hardware captures the emissions linked to the production, transportation, and disposal of the physical components, covering the carbon footprint across the manufacturing and lifecycle impacts of devices. Finally, the function unit provides a standardized measure of work, such as “per transaction” or “per user session,” enabling consistent comparisons across different systems based on output.

  • • The calculation of SCI score requires the analysis of IT infrastructure, code efficiency, energy consumption of servers, their geographical location, frequency and duration of operations, number of users and other factors that contribute to energy consumption. Based on the score, techniques can be engaged to mitigate the environmental impact of the considered software. In the next section we will present in detail a case study of a Fintech company that defined a CO2 emissions baseline using the SCI score.

  • • Sustainable Development Goal (SDG): SDG are a set of 17 global goals established by the United Nations in 2015 as part of 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. These goals are designed to address global challenges such as poverty, zero hunger, good health and well-being, quality education and so on. Particularly, goal 13 refers to the actions to be taken to combat climate change and its impacts. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change18 (IPCC) in 2021 shown that human emission of greenhouse gases due by human activities have contributed to approximately 1.1°C of global warming since the late 19th century (1850-1900). IPCC estimates that global temperature will rise by 1.5°C in the next two decades. However, these estimates were made before the AI era, in which supercomputers require more and more resources (energy and water) to train algorithms, and thus the expected global temperature could far exceed previous predictions. If appropriate measures are not implemented, the intensification of the water cycle is likely to occur with intended precipitation and associated flooding in high latitudes and rare rainfall in subtropical regions, rising ocean levels resulting in coastal erosion, more frequent marine heatwaves, ocean acidification, and rising temperatures in cities with serious consequences for infrastructure and public health.

  • • Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG)19: Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG) is a set of criteria that allows investors to evaluate corporate performance based not only on financial returns but also on environmental sustainability practices, social impacts and governance practices of a company. Private and certified companies assign an ESG score to other companies based on specific parameters.

  • • A low ESG score is associated with all companies adopting sustainability practices. The study conducted by Gupta et al. (2021) shows a statistical correlation between ESG values and financial values. Specifically:

  • • The average “return on investment” of a company with low ESG and high ESG is 5.4% and 2.93% respectively.

  • • The average “return on equity” of a company with low ESG and high ESG is 19.83% and 2.93% respectively.

  • • Decarbonizing the bank’s ICT infrastructure is a key aspect of the E component of ESG standards. The decarbonization process affects the entire ICT infrastructure: from the number of servers used to their geographical location, from the number of operations performed by users to the background consumption of the application. Although this process can be scary, expensive, and time-consuming, it can start with the decarbonization of new AI-based services. Greening AI techniques enable the Fintech sector to fulfill ESG regulation and mitigate climate change.

  • • European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)20: The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) officially came into force on January 5, 202321. This directive requires that European – and some non-European – companies and SMEs to produce a comprehensive report on sustainability. These reports must adopt a double materiality perspective – specifying how sustainability issues impact both the company’s financial performance and how the company’s operations affect environmental and social factors. The reporting must be in accordance with European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). ESRS are a set of principles established by the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group (EFRAG) to standardize how companies disclose information about their ESG impacts.

  • • Global Reporting Initiative (GRI)22: GRI Standard provides a comprehensive set of guidelines for companies to create reports that cover environmental, social and governance sustainability aspect. These standards are compatible with ESG principles and promote transparency and accountability of organizations regarding their sustainable impact.

3. LITERATURE REVIEW

In this section, we present the state of the art on Green Fintech and Green AI techniques. A general overview on the adoption of AI-based technologies in the Fintech domain will also help determine the number and types of use cases that could benefit from decarbonization efforts. Then, existing industry case studies related to Green AI in Fintech are reported. Finally the open issues motivating the writing of this book chapter are presented.

Green Fintech

The term “Green Fintech” appears for the first time in 2017 when United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) and Ant Group at the World Economic Forum launched the Green Digital Finance Alliance (GDFA), a no-profit foundation that enables and co-creates transformative digital and financial innovation for climate, nature and biodiversity challenges with a global ecosystem23 24. Green Fintech is the combination of financial technology and environmental sustainability and has two main goals. The first is to stimulate a green economy by offering services and capital. The second is to offer these services while reducing the environmental impact of these services as much as possible.

As confirmed by Google Trends, the interest on the Green Fintech topic has significantly grown from 2016 to date (Figure 2). The numbers in the y axis represent the search interest relative to the highest point of the graph in relation to the indicated region and period. The value 100 indicates the highest frequency of searches for the term, 50 indicates half of the searches. A score of 0, on the other hand, indicates that not enough data was collected for the term. Financial firms’ increasing interest on Green Fintech show that not only they are creating innovation in the sector, they also are looking more and more to do it wisely, i.e. with the environment in mind.

Figure 2. The growing number of web searches with the “Green Fintech” query

The Paris Agreement and the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) represent goals that nations must achieve to deal climate change, improve environmental sustainability and promote socio-economic growth. The Paris Agreement25, in article 2.c, invites countries to make “financial flows consistent with a path toward low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development and climate-resilient development”. Achieving these goals requires the application of new technologies that are more sustainable from an environmental perspective than those available today. This migration to new technologies requires large amounts of investments. The Trade and Development report presented during the United Nations Conference (2014) estimates total annual investment to $5 trillion-$7 trillion (Nassiry, 2018).

Although the investment required from banks and financial institutions to adopt sustainable technologies may discourage them, there is potential return on investment driven by increasing consumer awareness of climate change. As demonstrated by several studies, consumers are willing to pay a premium for services and products that are environmentally friendly (Biswas & Roy, 2016; Wei et al., 2018; Namkung & Jang, 2017). Furthermore, millennials are among the main drivers of Fintech and particularly interested in sustainable investments26 (Hosen et al., 2023; Srivastava et al., 2024).

The use of technology in the finance sector allows financial resources to be channeled to sustainable enterprises through lower-cost investments (Macchiavello & Siri., 2022). Blockchain, Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), AI, Big Data and Internet of Things (IoT) are being used to ensure transparency in supply chain, digital identity, financial inclusion, property rights, green trading platform and green crowdfunding and others green applications (Nassiry, 2018; Macchiavello & Siri, 2022). A question arises: how cost-effective is it really to deliver green services using a non-ecofriendly ICT infrastructure? Blockchain and DTLs require a non-negligible amount of energy to function correctly, and this energy impacts the environment in terms of CO2 emitted. The same goes for training of AI algorithms and all the other services.

AI in Fintech

The integration of AI in the Fintech sector is not just a trend but a great revolution affecting existing financial systems, design of future financial services and customer experience of consumers. Over the past 20 years, the scientific literature of AI applications in Fintech has expanded considerably (Bahoo et al., 2024; Biju et al., 2024). The reason is that AI significantly impacts how financial institutions manage security, regulatory compliance, anti-fraud measures, anti-money laundering (AML), and know-your-customer (KYC) policies (Bagó, 2023). However, the integration of AI in Fintech is not limited to this. Bahoo et al. (2024) conducted a comprehensive review identifying ten main research streams in which AI is applied: stock market, trading models, volatility forecasting, portfolio management, performance, risk and default evaluation, cryptocurrencies, derivatives, credit risk in banks, investor sentiment analysis and foreign exchange management. Aysan et al. (2024) applied Random Forest algorithm to investigate risk management in Islamic banks using data from 2016 to 2021. The Random Forest is widely used in classification and regression tasks. It is based on the combination of multiple decision trees to improve accuracy and robustness of predictions. The same algorithm was used by Zheng et al. (2024) for analyzing and forecasting the US stock market with a predictive accuracy of about 85-95%.

Beyond financial services, AI can be used to safeguard consumers, preventing credit card fraud, anomaly detection, protecting sensitive data and improving the overall customer experience. Lacruz & Saniie (2021) developed two different methods for fraud detection with a high level of accuracy: an Autoencoder (semi-supervised learning algorithm) and Logistic Regression (supervised learning algorithm). Distante et al. (2022) applied AI to improve the customer experience of consumers. In particular, the authors applied a modified version of U-net (Ronneberger et al., 2015) that exploits the user's purchasing habits to decide whether a purchase is typical or not, so that in the case of a typical purchase the Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) could be exempted. U-net is Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of performing anomaly detection using a reconstruction-error-based method ensuing high performance during training and evaluation phases. Aslan (2023) proposed an automated anomaly detector system for Token Financial Technologies, a Turkish Fintech, based on Isolation Forest algorithm. Isolation Forest is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm that isolates unusual data points rather than directly profiling typical data. This detection system enabled the company to prevent the deletion of over 55% of banking applications on devices during the last quarter of 2020.

The development and adoption of AI by banks is made possible by the extensive utilization of Big Data. Financial institutions have Big Data referred to transaction histories, customer habits, market trends etc., which can be used in the AI training process. The development of an AI algorithm for Fintech can be divided into four phases: data preparation, model selection, model training, validation and testing. In the data preparation phase, the available data are pre-processed to remove any errors, correct anomalies - such as missing values in incomplete transactions - and transformed into a normalized format or useful format for processing. In model selection phase, the most suitable technique and algorithm are chosen to solve the problem of interest. During the model training, the algorithm learns from the data by identifying patterns and relationships. The model’s parameters are fine-tuned and optimized to minimize error and improve the accuracy of its predictions. Fine-tuning refers to the process of specializing the model for a specific task - such as anomaly detection, financial predictions, user profiling etc. - using a smaller dataset than the training dataset. During validation and testing phase, the algorithm is run on data different from the training data to assess how it would perform in the production scenario. In the case of unsatisfactory performance, it is possible to go back to previous phases to identify and resolve any development errors or design choices. It is important to consider that choosing the model requires the exploration, study and testing of existing model architecture. This involves a considerable amount of time and computational resources, resulting in a significant environmental impact (Poenaru-Olaru et al., 2023a). Even starting the training phase on an incomplete or inappropriate dataset result in wasted time and resources, adding to the environmental impact.

As we will see in the next section, there are techniques that can mitigate this environmental impact without compromising accuracy or increasing processing time.

Green AI

In this section we summarize some of the results of a recent systematic review (Verdecchia et al., 2023), by analyzing the provided replication package27, which is accessible online under an open-source license. This study analyzes 98 peer-reviewed papers, highlighting a significant increase in research activity since 2020. The review offers a thorough summary of the key topics within Green AI literature, identifying 13 distinct areas of focus. Among these, the most attention is given to monitoring, hyperparameter tuning, model benchmarking, and deployment. On the other hand, less explored areas, such as data-centric approaches, estimation, and emissions, suggest potential research gaps that should be addressed in the future.

In Figure 3 we present the distribution of publications according to different Green AI definitions, based on the level of abstraction used to assess AI's environmental impact: energy efficiency (Verdecchia et al., 2021), carbon footprint (Wiedmann & Minx, 2008), or ecological footprint (Matuštík et al., 2021). The figure reveals that only 20 papers (approximately 22% of the primary studies) specifically address the AI carbon footprint. This is notable, as recent research (Luccioni & Hernandez-Garcia, 2023) highlights that reducing AI's environmental impact solely to energy consumption is an overly simplistic approach.

Figure 3. Number of publications per type of green AI definition

The 20 primary studies are divided into observational (Strubell et al., 2020; Dodge et al., 2022; Fraga-Lamas et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022; Ferro et al; 2023; Asperti et al., 2021; Jooste et al., 2021; Bannour et al., 2021), position (Tamburrini, 2022; Kaack et al., 2022; Willenbacker et al., 2021; Patterson et al., 2022; Ligozat et al., 2022; Dhar, 2020; Rohde e al., 2021), and solution-oriented papers (Wenninger et al., 2022; Henderson et al., 2020; Anthony et al., 2020; Lannelongue, 2021). Among these, the observational and solution papers are particularly relevant to this study, and we briefly summarize their content here.

Strubell et al. (2020) present a groundbreaking study evaluating the carbon impact of training state-of-the-art models, highlighting the pressing need to reduce the carbon footprint associated with AI development and deployment. Their work has initiated important discussions within the AI research community. Dodge et al. (2022) introduce the first benchmark of Flexible Start and Pause & Resume training strategies, which will be elaborated upon in the following section. Fraga-Lamas et al. (2021) examine the carbon footprint involved in the creation and use of AI systems, focusing specifically on the energy consumption in an AI-powered IoT scenario and reporting the resulting carbon emissions across different countries and energy sources. Wu et al. (2022) investigate the energy consumption of state-of-the-art models across their lifecycle, offering insights into AI's carbon footprint at Facebook. They reveal that roughly 50% of the total carbon cost of AI models is due to the embodied carbon in the hardware used for model development, while also noting that GPUs are significantly underutilized, operating at only 30-50% of their capacity in most training workflows. Ferro et al. (2023) conduct experiments on twenty-seven datasets using two decision tree algorithms and two ensemble methods for classification and regression tasks, assessing the energy efficiency of these ML algorithms and the impact of design parameters on energy consumption. Asperti et al. (2021) evaluate the energy costs associated with various variational autoencoders, providing a useful benchmark for comparing the energy footprint of different models and training techniques. Jooste et al. (2022) demonstrate how model distillation techniques can make machine translation systems more sustainable. In a simulated low-resource German-to-English translation task, they show that distilled student models can cut emissions and costs by nearly 50%. Finally, Bannour et al. (Bannour, 2021) review tools for measuring the energy consumption and CO2 emissions of Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods. They compare six tools –carbon tracker, experiment impact tracker, Green algorithms, ML CO2 impact, energy usage, and cumulator – using named entity recognition experiments across different computational environments (local server vs. computing facility).

With regards to solution papers, Wenninger et al. (2022) faces the challenge of extending ML approaches to include the application’s energy consumption. They present the Sustainable Machine Learning Balance Sheet as a framework allowing them to holistically evaluate and develop sustainable ML solutions. The framework was validated in a case study and through expert interviews. Henderson et al. (2020) promote accounting as a means to incentivize energy-efficient research. They develop a leaderboard by providing a simple interface for tracking real-time energy consumption and carbon emissions. Finally, based on case studies using the framework, they propose strategies for mitigation of carbon emissions and reduction of energy consumption. Anthony et al. (2020) propose that energy and carbon footprint of model development and training should be reported alongside performance metrics using tools like Carbontracker, which is aimed at tracking and predicting the energy and carbon footprint of training DL models. Lannelongue et al. (2021) present a methodological framework to estimate the carbon footprint of any computational task in a standardized and reliable way, as well as defining metrics to contextualize GHG emissions. They provide tool which is freely available online28 enabling user to estimate and report the carbon footprint of their computation.

The briefly reported studies contain the most recent advancements in the field of Green AI that can be useful for the financial industry to decarbonize their algorithms and to take wiser decisions when setting up new AI-based projects.

Case Studies

Currently, it can be observed a lack of documentation on initiatives by financial institutions moving into the field of Green Software and Green Fintech. Nevertheless, it this section we collect and describe the few existing industrial efforts documented on the web.

In 2023, the European Central Bank (ECB) conducted a study on the environmental footprint of euro banknotes29. According to the report, 37% of the environmental impact of banknotes is due to ATM energy consumption, 35% to transportation, 10% to distribution, 9% to paper production, and 5% to verification activities at physical locations. In 2024, Auriga, an Italian software house for multi-channel banking (with worldwide branches), published an opinion paper on how to reduce emissions for cash handling and access30. According to Auriga, banks should invest in new machines that consume less energy and are equipped with intelligent energy management features, such as low-energy LED lighting, ambient light detection, and more efficient modules with smarter power supplies and electronics. The paper also says that the distribution of cash to bank branches and ATMs ranks as the second-largest contributor to the carbon footprint of physical cash, following the energy consumption of ATMs. Therefore, it is crucial to find ways to make cash distribution more environmentally efficient. This involves addressing the physical methods of distribution, with a focus on how Cash-in-Transit (CIT) vehicles can reduce fuel consumption or operate on zero-emission fuels, such as electricity or green hydrogen. Additionally, the carbon footprint of physical cash can be minimized by using smarter cash management systems that optimize cash deliveries, thus reducing the emissions associated with supplying ATMs with cash. The use of predictive analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning for real-time monitoring of cash withdrawals and deposits enables a more sustainable management strategy by allowing for more accurate demand forecasting. AI can analyze the entire ATM network to determine the ideal locations, services, and cash levels for each machine, optimizing the overall network management strategy. Additionally, AI-driven optimization of cash transportation routes and frequencies can help reduce carbon emissions. Auriga is already helping banks to be more sustainable by offering an AI-based service named WWS Cash Management. WWS Cash Management31 is a backend module able to optimize the entire cash management process for banks and financial institutions. Its algorithm is trained using a 12-month dataset of cash requirements and movements and enables banks to reduce cash handling costs by 10 to 25%.

Another study proposed by Accenture32 found that only 12% of the world's banks are on the right track to reduce emissions from their own operations. In addition, IT infrastructure not only requires a lot of electricity but also water resources for cooling systems. Finally, also ING Bank has proven commitment towards the environmental problem by publishing a report33 in which it is shown that global water consumption has increased from 738 million liters in 2015 to more than 840 million in 2021.

A case study published by UBS34, the world’s leading wealth manager, is the only documented case where a bank has proactively established a baseline of carbon emissions generated by its software. UBS has teamed up with the Green Software Foundation to quantify the environmental impact of two of two applications, Investment Bank app and Asset Management app, using the SCI score. Before moving on practical use case, we define:

  • • Energy: it is the maximum energy used by the hardware. This data is obtained from all servers in the central application database.

  • • Resource Share: how much of the hardware is used by the software. his data is captured in the central application database, and for Virtual Machine can be derived from the hardware usage data.

  • • Operating Time: it is the time in which the server is actively running to support the app's services. In the study, the authors assumed the software is running 365 days a year, 24 hours a day (8760 hours).

For the Investment Bank app and Asset Management app, the process involves calculating total CO2 Operational Emissions both per hour and per year, representing the emissions generated during the app's runtime (Table 2 and Table 3). Additionally, the process includes calculating the total CO2 Embodied Emissions per server that host the app (Table 4). Finally, it calculates the total CO2 Embodied Emissions of the application itself (Table 5). Carbon Intensity data was obtained from the national grid of the country where the datacenters were located.
