2. REVIEW OF LITERATURE

Data analytics is becoming increasingly integral to modern internal audit practices, offering the potential to enhance audit quality, refine risk assessment techniques, and optimize decision-making processes. Its impact spans across various sectors, including finance, healthcare, and technology. Each sector presents unique challenges, opportunities, and specific approaches to integrating data analytics within audit processes.

Consulting firms, supported by scholarly articles and industry reports, play a pivotal role in advancing the use of data analytics in internal audits. They introduce methodologies, frameworks, tools, and techniques that facilitate the implementation of data analytics pipelines within client organizations. This growing trend underscores the importance of data analytics in improving audit efficiency and effectiveness.

Particularly in heavily regulated industries such as healthcare and finance, the need for robust data governance strategies is paramount. Effective data governance must align with the regulatory environment to ensure compliance and mitigate risks. The literature review highlights real-world case studies, showcasing successful applications of data analytics in internal audit departments, demonstrating the tangible benefits and outcomes of this transformative approach.

The study of Alles & Gray (2016) reveals that corporate investment in Big Data reached $34 billion in 2013, with projections suggesting this figure would soar to $232 billion by 2016. The Big Four accounting firms are at the forefront of integrating Big Data into their practices, especially as it becomes essential to their assurance processes. Although Big Data has seen substantial progress in fields such as marketing and healthcare, its application in auditing is still in the early stages. The study emphasizes the barriers hindering the widespread adoption of Big Data in financial statement audits and proposes a research agenda to tackle these challenges. In line with this, Brazel et al. (2013) offer insights into how auditors approach fraud detection and decision-making, revealing that a minority of auditors rely on Non-Financial Measures (NFMs) for testing, even when fraud red flags are identified. Their findings also suggest that high fraud risk alone is insufficient to trigger a deeper review of inconsistent NFMs, though auditors can be more effective when prompted appropriately. Additionally, a shift towards a more collaborative, coaching-style approach in internal auditing—rather than a “police officer” mentality—has been shown to increase agreement with internal auditors’ recommendations, especially when minor errors are overlooked (Brown & Fanning, 2018). These insights highlight how both traditional auditing approaches and new technological advances like Big Data must evolve together to enhance auditing practices and effectiveness.

Interestingly, managers tend to trust in-house internal auditors' suggestions, even when they conflict with their preferences, particularly when these suggestions are quantified. In contrast, managers show less trust in external auditors (Burton et al., 2012). Internal auditors who act as a Management Training Ground (MTG) are seen as more competent, and this study (Carcello et al., 2018) is the first to show that using internal audit as an MTG can have beneficial effects, contrary to previous reports.

The impact of internal auditors on managerial decisions has been significant, with the practitioner literature suggesting that a “policeman approach” often damages relationships due to the lack of client service incentives seen in external audits. This tension has substantial implications for internal auditors, management, external auditors, and corporate governance (Fanning & Piercey, 2014). Auditing reforms have been proposed worldwide, addressing contentious issues such as ethics, independence, social and environmental accounting, and the future of auditing. These developments are vital for lawmakers, regulators, professionals, students, and researchers in auditing and accounting (Hay et al., 2014).

In auditing, preference reversal (PR) occurs when decision makers evaluate choices differently depending on whether they are assessed jointly or separately (Hsee, 1996). This theory suggests that PRs emerge because some choice characteristics are easier to evaluate when assessed separately, while others are more challenging. Decision makers often use various visualization tools to analyze large datasets across different domains, such as marketing and sales. Lurie & Mason (2006) highlight how visual representations can influence decision-making by marketing managers and consumers, especially in contexts involving data analysis or synthesis. Such representations can enhance efficiency, provide new insights, and increase customer satisfaction, though they can also introduce biases.

A study by Moffitt et al. (2016) supplements a 2015 American Accounting Association panel on the history and future of Accounting Information Systems (AIS) research. It identifies key research topics in top AIS journals and predicts future research trends over the next 30 years. Similarly, Stippich (2016) explores how audit leaders are integrating data mining and analytics to optimize audit department impact and efficiency. His research aims to develop a data analytics platform to enhance risk coverage, improve audit efficiency, and reduce duplication in data mining efforts. The collaboration between the IIA Research Foundation and Grant Thornton provided subject matter expertise for this study, which looks into how internal auditors' performance reputations influence corporate managers' trust (Tang et al., 2017).

In the realm of internal audit effectiveness, projects leveraging data analytics vary across sectors, each with specific aims and objectives tailored to their unique challenges. For instance, in the finance sector, projects like “Fraud Detection and Prevention Enhancement” use advanced statistical analysis and machine learning algorithms to identify abnormal patterns and potential fraud within financial transactions. In healthcare, initiatives such as “Billing and Claims Audit Optimization” employ various data analytics techniques to improve the accuracy of billing activities, detect coding irregularities, and prevent revenue loss, ensuring compliance with regulations like HIPAA. Meanwhile, in the technology sector, projects like “IT Controls Assessment and Optimization” focus on analyzing system logs, network traffic, and user access patterns to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities and bolster information security measures.

In the consulting industry, initiatives like the “Internal Audit Transformation Initiative” aim to assess existing processes and implement data analytics solutions, adopting a risk-based audit approach to enhance audit quality, streamline operations, and provide value through data-driven insights. These sector-specific projects underscore the transformative potential of data analytics in enhancing internal audit effectiveness, mitigating risks, and fostering organizational resilience in an increasingly complex business environment.

In addition to industry-specific initiatives, organizations across various sectors are now adopting cross-functional data analytics projects designed to continuously improve and innovate internal audit practices. These initiatives typically involve collaboration among internal audit teams, IT departments, and data analytics specialists, who work together to create customized, tailor-made solutions that meet the specific needs and objectives of the organization. Through strategic partnerships and interdisciplinary cooperation, organizations can leverage data analytics to enhance audit efficiency, optimize risk management strategies, and unlock new opportunities for value creation.

By fostering a data-driven decision-making culture and promoting continuous learning, organizations position themselves to thrive in an ever-evolving business landscape. In this context, the ability to effectively leverage data analytics has become a key determinant of competitive advantage and organizational success. Relevant ongoing research in fields such as Artificial Intelligence (Patil et al., 2024; Prabhu, Nandanwar, et al., 2024; Prabhu, Kanse, et al., 2024), Cybersecurity (Anand et al., 2023; Prabhu et al., 2024; Ravindranathan et al., 2024), Cloud Computing (Saxena et al., 2024), and Chatbots (Waghambare et al., 2023; M. Waghambare et al., 2024) further contributes to both financial and non-financial aspects of business operations, driving innovation and strengthening internal audit functions.

3. THE IMPACT OF DATA ANALYTICS ON INTERNAL AUDIT WORKFLOW

Data analytics has significantly reshaped the internal audit workflow, enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and the ability to mitigate risk. The introduction of data analytics tools into auditing practices has led to more comprehensive, real-time insights, improving each step of the traditional audit process. Below, we explore how data analytics has transformed key stages of the internal audit workflow summarized in Figure 3.

Figure 3. Workflow process in internal audit

In the initial stage of setting audit objectives, data analytics has replaced traditional approaches reliant on manual scoping and limited insights. By leveraging historical data and previous audit reports, auditors can identify patterns, prioritize high-risk areas, and focus their efforts on potential vulnerabilities. Predictive models further refine these objectives, offering foresight into emerging risks and ensuring alignment with broader organizational strategies.

The process of understanding data sources, once labor-intensive and fragmented, has been streamlined by data analytics tools. Auditors can now integrate and analyze data from diverse sources, including financial transactions, operational databases, and external feeds, using advanced aggregation platforms. This seamless integration ensures that data is not only accessible but also reliable, accurate, and timely. Automated validation and error-checking capabilities eliminate human errors, securing data integrity as the foundation for effective audits.

Data preparation, traditionally a time-consuming task involving manual cleaning, transforming, and reconciling of data, has been significantly optimized. Automation through data analytics tools identifies and resolves errors, removes inconsistencies, and ensures compatibility across various data formats. These platforms further enhance data integrity by automating reconciliation processes, reducing preparation time, and delivering accurate and complete datasets ready for analysis.

At the core of the internal audit workflow lies data analysis, a stage that has been completely transformed by analytics. In contrast to manual sampling methods that often missed critical insights, data analytics enables exhaustive, real-time examination of large datasets. Advanced techniques such as descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive analytics uncover patterns, trends, and anomalies, empowering auditors to detect fraud, compliance violations, and inefficiencies. Machine learning algorithms and statistical tools enhance this phase, allowing auditors to generate actionable insights with greater precision and speed.

The reporting phase has also seen a significant evolution. Data analytics tools facilitate the presentation of findings in visually compelling formats, including dashboards, graphs, and heat maps, which make complex insights accessible to stakeholders. This level of clarity and context promotes informed decision-making and encourages collaboration between auditors and management. Enhanced visualization of key metrics and trends enables organizations to take timely and effective actions, integrating audit results seamlessly into business strategies.

Overall, data analytics has elevated internal audit workflows, transitioning them from manual, fragmented processes to integrated, data-driven methodologies. By enhancing planning, streamlining data preparation, enabling exhaustive analysis, and refining reporting, data analytics not only improves operational efficiency but also delivers strategic value to organizations. This transformation underscores the critical role of analytics in modernizing the internal audit function and aligning it with the demands of today’s complex business environment.

4. THE TREND OF INTEGRATING DATA ANALYTICS

Data analytics has become an essential tool in the internal audit function, evolving from a technical asset to a cornerstone of decision-making and risk management. By leveraging the power of analytics, internal auditors can now provide real-time, actionable insights that drive organizational improvements. Traditional audit models, reliant on sampling and manual processes, have been replaced by data-driven approaches that offer more comprehensive, accurate, and timely results. As organizations continue to generate vast amounts of data, the role of data analytics in internal audit is expected to grow even further, helping businesses stay ahead of emerging risks and improve operational efficiency.

4.1 Shifting the Audit Paradigm: From Traditional to Data-Driven Approaches

The increasing complexity of the business environment and the growing need for more agile audit processes make data analytics indispensable. By providing a more granular, holistic view of organizational operations, data analytics helps internal auditors identify hidden risks, improve compliance, and ensure that operations align with strategic goals. This shift not only enhances the accuracy of audits but also enables auditors to add more value by identifying opportunities for process improvement, cost savings, and risk mitigation. As businesses face a more complex landscape, data analytics adoption is crucial in detecting risks and gaining insights into organizational operations, which can significantly inform management decisions.

4.2 Data Analytics as a Conceptual Framework for Risk Management

The integration of data analytics into internal audit functions goes beyond just technological implementation; it represents a fundamental shift in how audits are approached. Data analytics should be viewed as a conceptual framework that enables organizations to extract actionable insights from diverse data streams to support decision-making and risk management processes. This framework allows auditors to identify risks proactively and make informed decisions based on comprehensive data analysis. The exponential growth in data volume and diversity—comprising both structured and unstructured data—has made it increasingly challenging for traditional audit methods to keep up. Conventional audit techniques, such as sampling, provide only a partial view of the risks within operational processes, often overlooking important outliers and control weaknesses.

4.3 Data Analytics in Managing Modern Risks

Today’s business environment operates within a complex financial and information system, where detailed analysis of data is crucial. Instead of relying on a small sample subset, comprehensive data analysis paints a fuller picture of potential risks and weaknesses. Internal audit functions are under pressure to be more efficient, identifying risks early, responding promptly, and providing valuable insights into organizational operations. By adopting data analytics, internal auditors can meet these rising demands, improving efficiency, accuracy, and effectiveness in their risk assessments. This approach also enhances organizational resilience by identifying and mitigating risks before they escalate.

4.4 Application of Data Analytics in Internal Audit Functions

Data analytics is increasingly applied across various functional areas in internal audit, particularly in transactional areas like expenditure management, payroll, and accounts payable. These areas, governed by clear rules and processes, offer the best opportunities for identifying errors, cost-saving opportunities, and potential fraud. By analyzing tracking data, auditors can verify billing accuracy and assess compliance with contractual obligations. Sophisticated tools like IDEA and ACL simplify the sampling process, allowing auditors to determine the right sample size and composition, which supports defensible inferences when applied to entire populations rather than just samples.

4.5 Payroll and Employee Expense Monitoring

Payroll management presents significant risks, including ghost employees, forged wage claims, and tampered timesheets. Data analytics provides a means of identifying these threats early, allowing organizations to maintain financial integrity and ensure compliance. Specific applications include:

  • • Ghost Employee Detection: Identifying employees listed on payroll who no longer work for the organization by analyzing discrepancies in personal information.

  • • Post-Employment Payments: Tracking payments to employees after they have resigned to prevent unauthorized transactions.

  • • Unapproved Time Entries: Detecting unauthorized time entries that could lead to overpayments.

  • • Payroll Analysis: Reviewing payroll data for anomalies, such as excessive overtime, to identify areas of concern.

  • • Expense Claim Monitoring: Ensuring that expense claims are within approval limits and identifying potential fraud.

These techniques not only help mitigate financial risks but also ensure compliance with organizational policies and regulations.

4.6 Enhancing Revenue and Accounts Receivable Audits

Data analytics plays a critical role in auditing revenue streams and invoicing processes, especially in industries with large volumes of data, such as telecommunications and utilities. By using data analytics to verify billing accuracy across large datasets, auditors can more effectively detect errors and discrepancies that may go unnoticed in traditional sampling approaches. Similarly, in accounts receivable, data analytics can help identify issues such as duplicate invoices, missing receipts, or bad debts. By uncovering weaknesses in the credit control process, auditors can provide valuable insights for improving financial management and reducing risks.

5. BENEFITS OF DATA ANALYTICS IN INTERNAL AUDIT

Benefits and challenges around data analytics in internal audit span a wide list of factors that are fundamental for companies desiring to implement analytics proficiently in order to strengthen audit processes, identify risks and create business value. This exhaustive review explains the main pluses and minuses of the integration of analytics into internal audits.

  • • Enhanced Risk Identification and Assessment

Internal auditors utilize data analytics for the purpose of analyzing a huge volume of data from different sources. This enables the identification and evaluation of risks in a more comprehensive way. Through applying advanced analytics techniques, fraud auditors can identify recurring patterns, uncommon cases, and emerging trends which represent risks and then take preventive and corrective measures.

  • • Improved Audit Efficiency and Effectiveness:

The use of data analytics ensures that manual processes are automated, the tasks that are repetitive are eliminated, and audit procedures are accelerated; this increases audit efficiency and effectiveness. Through the use of analytics tools for data extraction, cleansing and analysis auditors can concentrate on the more value-adding tasks of risk assessment, identification of the root cause, and strategic decision support, thereby resource optimization and better audit outcomes will be achieved.

  • • Enhanced Fraud Detection and Prevention

Data analytics allows internal auditors to detect and prevent fraud with more effectiveness by scrutinizing transactional data, identifying discrepancies, and uncovering patterns that are indicative of fraudulent activity. Through utilization of predictive analytics models and anomaly detection techniques, audit function can do a proactive identification of potential fraud risks, solidifying the internal controls, and reducing the financial losses.

  • • Optimized Resource Allocation and Prioritization:

Data analytics through internal audit functions allows them to prioritize their audit activates, allocate resources in the most efficient manner, and identify the areas of the highest risk and impact. Auditors perform ongoing risk-based assessments and leverage data analytics to plan and strategize audits according to specific objectives, standards, and new risks, and to maximize the efficiency of resources and coverage.

6. DATA ANALYTICS CONSULTING IN INTERNAL AUDIT

Data analytics consulting in internal audit has become an essential service for organizations navigating increasingly complex business environments. With challenges such as evolving regulatory requirements, rapid technological advancements, and massive volumes of data, consulting firms offer valuable guidance in optimizing internal audit processes through the use of data analytics. These firms help businesses harness the power of analytics to streamline operations, enhance decision-making, and strengthen risk management strategies. The primary aim of consulting firms is to align data analytics with the strategic objectives of the organization, enabling businesses to optimize resources and promote sustainable growth.

One of the focuses for consulting firms is ensuring that data analytics initiatives are closely aligned with the organization’s strategic goals and risk management priorities. By understanding the client’s objectives, compliance needs, and risk profiles, consultants tailor analytics models to address specific business challenges. This strategic alignment not only helps organizations improve resource management but also facilitates better decision-making and ensures that internal audit processes are aligned with the company’s long-term vision.

In addition to strategic alignment, consulting firms emphasize the integration of advanced analytics technologies into the internal audit function. They work with clients to assess existing infrastructure and identify gaps, then help implement cutting-edge analytics platforms capable of handling large volumes of data from various sources. Whether through data visualization tools, predictive models, or machine learning algorithms, consultants ensure that organizations have access to state-of-the-art technologies, allowing them to make data-driven decisions and optimize their internal audit processes.

Risk assessment and prioritization are also key elements in the consulting viewpoint on data analytics in internal audit. Consultants stress the importance of adopting a risk-based approach to auditing, which helps organizations prioritize audit activities based on the likelihood and impact of risks. By using data analytics to assess both inherent and residual risks across various business functions, consultants enable organizations to enhance their risk management capabilities and strengthen internal controls, thereby preventing potential issues before they arise.

Moreover, data quality and governance are crucial for the success of any data analytics initiative. Consulting firms help clients establish robust data management frameworks, develop comprehensive data governance policies, and implement quality assurance processes. Ensuring data accuracy, integrity, and transparency throughout the data lifecycle is essential for generating reliable analytics outputs that inform decision-making and ensure regulatory compliance.

Consulting firms also recognize the importance of developing internal capabilities within organizations to support data-driven internal audits. They offer tailored training programs to equip internal auditors with the necessary skills and expertise in data analytics tools and techniques. By fostering a culture of continuous learning and improvement, consultants help organizations maximize the return on their investment in analytics and drive ongoing enhancements in internal audit practices.

Finally, consultants emphasize the need for continuous monitoring and refinement of data analytics processes. They provide organizations with key performance indicators (KPIs), metrics, and benchmarks to measure the impact of analytics on internal audit efficiency and effectiveness. Through regular evaluations and feedback mechanisms, consulting firms help organizations identify areas for optimization and innovation, ensuring that the internal audit function remains agile and responsive to evolving business needs.

In conclusion, successful implementation of data analytics in internal audit requires strategic alignment, integration of advanced technologies, thorough risk assessment, robust data governance, skills development, and ongoing process improvement. Consulting firms play a pivotal role in guiding organizations through these steps, helping them create a more efficient, effective, and data-driven internal audit function that adds value and mitigates risk in a rapidly changing business environment.

7. CHALLENGES OF DATA ANALYTICS IN INTERNAL AUDIT

  • • Data Quality and Integrity

The main risk in data analytics for internal audit is ensuring data quality, integrity, and dependability. Inaccurate, incomplete, or biased data can make outputs of analytics biased and thus lead to inaccurate inferences. Internal auditors must deploy modern data management frameworks, data cleaning methods and validation processes to mitigate data integrity issues along the analytics lifecycle.

  • • Technological Complexity and Integration

The introduction of data analytics technologies is a complex process which involves their integration into the existing audit process. The organizations may experience hard times while selecting right analytics tools, configuring data infrastructure, and integrating different data sources. Internal audit staff must be properly equipped with technical knowledge and teaming with IT personnel and external vendors to sidestep technological obstacles and create a smooth application of analytics solutions.

  • • Skills and Talent Gap

Data analytics involves a competence in statistical analysis, data manipulation, programming language, and also data visualization. In these cases, auditors could be using analytics tools ineffectively or not act on the information they derive from them. Organizations should always allocate resources in the professional development programs that will help to build internal capabilities and cultivate a culture of data-driven decision-making, close any skills and talent shortage existing in the audit function.

  • • Data Privacy and Security Concerns

Data analytics raises a lot of privacy, confidentiality, and security concerns, in particular if such data is personal or a sensitive, which it often is when it comes to data transfer over the Internet. And that is only one of the many parts of the problem. Organizations should follow the regulatory requirements, industry standard, and best practices in data privacy and security to avoid data breaches, unauthorized access, and also mishandling of any confidential information. Internal auditors should implement strong data governance frameworks, encryption protocols, and also authorization controls in place to ensure the security of sensitive data and reduce privacy risks.

  • • Interpretation and Actionability of Insights

Data analytics expertise consists only in the very first step. So, in the next step – the auditors should understand the data analysis outputs and then ratify them to create the recommendations. Appreciating the business context, detecting the real issues and reporting clearly are the basic requirements of the driving change and enhancing the organizational performance. Cooperation among the auditors, stakeholders, and managers and also presenting the findings in a comprehensible manner is very important for data analytics to provide appreciable results for the business.

Overall, data analytics offer numerous advantages for internal audit, including enhanced risk discovery, improved efficiency, fraud detection, resource optimization, and better compliance with regulations. However, companies must also address several challenges, such as data quality, technological complexities, skills development, data privacy, and the interpretation of insights, in order to fully realize the potential of data analytics within their internal audit functions.

8. REGULATORY AND COMPLIANCE CONSIDERATIONS

Data analysis based internal audit requires a holistic approach which keeps in mind the variances of various regulations, management practices, privacy factor, reporting requirements and adaptability to the changing regulations. Now we will look at these elements one by one.

  • • Regulatory Frameworks and Standards

Internal audit departments should have a deep knowledge of the regulatory requirements that pertain to the industry and region where it is located. This covers the knowledge of the relevant laws, e.g. Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) for the publicly traded organizations, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for the processing of personal data of EU citizens, or industry-specific regulations such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) for the healthcare organizations. Adherence to these regulations ensures that the data analytics processes are legally compliant and meet the regulatory expectations.

  • • Data Privacy and Confidentiality

As privacy of data becomes a very critical focus, internal auditors should ensure that data analytics projects are consistent with the strict standard of privacy and confidentiality. It means putting in place a mechanism to protect sensitive information and anonymizing or pseudonymizing the data where possible, while also ensuring compliance with data protection laws like the GDPR, CCPA, and many others. Auditors should monitor the data access controls, encryption protocols, and also data usage policies to ensure the confidential data is secure.

  • • Data Retention and Storage

Frequently reflecting the regulations dictate how long some specific type of data should be stored and in what shape. The internal auditors must formulate a strict data retention policy in order to comply with the regulations and with the company policies. They ought to guarantee that the data storage solutions are secure, also scaling, and capable of preserving the data for the specified period of time. Auditing data retention periodically is critical in keeping up with the regulatory requirements and avoiding the security risks posed by data storage and also archiving.

  • • Audit Trail and Documentation

Maintaining an entire audit trial is very crucial for the proof of compliance with the legal rules. Auditors of internal process should document all the aspects of data processing, such as methodology, assumptions, transformations, and also results. The documentation is proof of due diligence in the audit activities and lends credibility to the regulators to see during the audits. The strength of the audit trail management ensures accountability and integrity in the audit function.

  • • Regulatory Reporting and Disclosure

Integrating data analytics and organizational audits necessitates accountable and also compliant regulations. Besides, internal audit teams have to handle a large number of law regulations, for example, rules like SOX, GDPR and also others that are set policies, so that various data analysis and other operational processes will be based on the laws and comply with the legal requirements and expectations of regulators. This means implementing strict measures for data privacy and confidentiality as well as devising clear data retention and storage policies and maintaining complete audit trails tracking all activities executed under data analytics procedures. Internal auditors help to stay compliant by maintaining strong regulatory standards, which increases the trust in the organization with the regulators and also stakeholders and shows the commitment of the organization to regulatory matters.

  • • Pro-Active Monitoring

Additionally, the internal auditors should be pro-active in monitoring the changes of regulatory environment and transforming their practices to meet the new requirements. Regulatory landscapes are very dynamic, with the laws and regulations evolving continuously according to the time required, a proactive approach towards the regulatory change management is very much needed. Internal audit teams need to constantly assess the evolving regulatory environment, scrutinize those updates critically, and modify the compliance framework accordingly to reflect such changes. Embodying flexibility and agility in the audit process of responding to the changes in the regulation results in audit practices that are compliant with the current regulations, industry standards, and the best practices, hence, the quality of the audit is enhanced, and the organization's resilience to the changes within the regulatory environment is also enhanced.

In nutshell, regulatory and compliance concerns are the cornerstone to the deployment of data analytics, in terms of the internal audit departments’ success. Through taking an initiative to comply with regulatory requirements, protecting the data privacy as well as managing data retention and storage properly, preserving audit trails in full, helping in regulatory reporting, and keeping pace with the changing regulations, internal auditors can improve the audit quality, minimize compliance risks and maintain organizational integrity under the framework of a much-changing regulatory environment. Undeniably, data analytics collection may appear to be difficult at first, but it does not have to be a challenge you cannot master. That can be done through applying the existing tools and making gradual steps for bringing the analytics in the audit events. Data collection and analysis will be more effective if specific objectives are stated for data gathering and analysis; also, it becomes systematic ensuring the analytics results will add value in every audit cycle.

9. FUTURE TRENDS OF DATA ANALYTICS TECHNOLOGY IN FINANCIAL AUDITING

The integration of emerging technologies is reshaping the internal audit landscape, offering significant advancements in risk management, operational efficiency, and the depth of insights auditors can derive from organizational data. These technologies, ranging from artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to blockchain and advanced data analytics, are not only transforming traditional audit functions but also enabling a more proactive, data-driven approach to auditing that drives better decision-making and organizational resilience.

9.1 Integration of AI and ML Technologies

One of the most notable technologies revolutionizing internal audit is Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). These tools enable auditors to analyze complete datasets in real-time, identifying complex patterns that traditional sampling methods might miss. With the ability to automate routine tasks such as transaction testing, document reviews, and compliance checks, AI reduces human error and enhances the accuracy and efficiency of audits. Machine learning, in particular, continuously learns from historical data, developing predictive models that anticipate potential risks, including compliance violations, financial irregularities, and operational inefficiencies. This allows auditors to focus on higher-value tasks, such as strategic risk assessment and decision-making, rather than routine data processing. By leveraging these technologies, internal audits are evolving from reactive to proactive, with predictive risk modelling and anomaly detection now at the forefront of audit practices.

9.2 Robotic Process Automation

Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is another technology making significant strides in internal audits. RPA allows the automation of repetitive, rule-based tasks with precision and consistency. For instance, RPA bots are used to extract and validate data across multiple systems, perform continuous transaction testing, and generate comprehensive audit logs - all without human intervention. This reduces the manual workload on auditors, increases the speed and accuracy of audits, and enables more extensive coverage of financial and operational systems. With RPA working around the clock, audits are conducted continuously, eliminating delays associated with traditional audit cycles and providing real-time insights into an organization’s risk posture.

Advanced Data Analytics Platforms are increasingly being employed to convert raw data into actionable insights. These platforms aggregate and process vast amounts of data from diverse sources, allowing auditors to create dynamic dashboards that highlight potential risks, operational inefficiencies, and performance trends. Real-time monitoring capabilities enable continuous auditing, meaning auditors can identify irregularities as they arise. Furthermore, these platforms leverage sophisticated statistical algorithms and machine learning techniques to uncover subtle patterns and generate predictive models, providing auditors with unparalleled accuracy in risk assessment and fraud detection. This shift towards data-driven auditing ensures that internal audit teams can offer more valuable insights into organizational performance and governance.

9.3 Blockchain and Depenalization

Blockchain technology is also making its mark in internal auditing by providing an immutable, transparent, and decentralized ledger of transactions. Each transaction recorded on a blockchain is cryptographically secured, creating a tamper-proof audit trail that ensures the integrity of the data and eliminates the risk of unauthorized modifications. This is especially beneficial for auditing financial transactions, supply chains, and contractual agreements, where transparency and traceability are crucial. Moreover, smart contracts—automated contracts triggered by predefined conditions—are streamlining compliance verification and audit processes. By enabling real-time verification of transactions, blockchain technology ensures that auditors have access to a complete, tamper-proof historical record, enhancing the accuracy and reliability of audits.

9.4 Cloud-Based Audit Management Systems

Cloud-Based Audit Management Systems are becoming a cornerstone of modern internal audit operations. These platforms centralize data storage and enhance collaboration among audit teams, particularly those spread across multiple locations. By offering secure, scalable infrastructure, cloud-based systems enable real-time access to audit documentation, workpapers, and audit trails, improving workflow and decision-making. Advanced encryption, multi-factor authentication, and automated backup mechanisms ensure that audit data remains secure, while seamless integration with enterprise software enables automatic data synchronization and performance tracking. This centralized approach not only improves the efficiency and security of audits but also facilitates enhanced collaboration between audit teams, making it easier to manage complex, multi-location audits.

10. INDUSTRIAL INSIGHTS AND FUTURE TRENDS

Looking toward the future, predictive analytics is set to become a key component of internal audit strategies. By analyzing historical data, predictive models can forecast potential future risks, financial anomalies, and compliance issues before they materialize. This proactive approach allows auditors to allocate resources more efficiently, prioritize high-risk areas, and develop preemptive mitigation strategies. As predictive analytics tools continue to evolve, they are expected to integrate even more advanced machine learning techniques to improve risk forecasting accuracy and provide real-time, dynamic risk assessments. The ability to anticipate and address issues before they arise will position internal auditors as integral contributors to organizational strategy, rather than just risk assessors.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is another emerging technology that promises to further enhance internal auditing. NLP allows auditors to analyze unstructured textual data, such as contracts, emails, and communication logs, to uncover potential risks or compliance violations that might be overlooked through traditional manual reviews. NLP algorithms can classify and categorize documents, perform sentiment analysis, and detect semantic patterns, providing auditors with deeper insights into organizational communications. This capability will enable auditors to automate document review processes, reduce time spent on manual analysis, and uncover hidden risks faster. As NLP technology matures, it is expected to expand its role in contract analysis, compliance verification, and even the detection of emerging risks through the analysis of corporate communications.

Cybersecurity analytics is also emerging as an increasingly critical tool for internal auditors. As organizations face more sophisticated cyber threats, the ability to monitor digital security landscapes in real-time has become essential. Using machine learning, cybersecurity analytics tools can detect vulnerabilities, unauthorized access attempts, and potential breaches with remarkable speed and accuracy. These tools can create dynamic risk profiles, predict potential threats, and automate incident response mechanisms, enabling internal auditors to take a more proactive role in cybersecurity risk management. Moving forward, these analytics tools will likely become more integrated with overall audit functions, providing auditors with real-time insights into both financial and digital risks, and allowing for comprehensive risk assessments that span both operational and cybersecurity domains.

The trend toward continuous monitoring and assurance is another area where emerging technologies are expected to play a significant role in the future of internal auditing. By adopting monitoring systems that assess key risk indicators and transactional data in real-time, auditors will be able to conduct audits that are not confined to periodic cycles, but rather provide ongoing insights into the organization’s risk landscape. This shift will allow auditors to identify and address issues as they emerge, significantly improving the responsiveness and relevance of audit processes. As continuous monitoring tools become more sophisticated, they will be able to integrate predictive capabilities and real-time alerts, further enhancing audit efficiency and responsiveness.

11. CONCLUSION

To sum up, the integration of data analytics into internal audit processes represents a revolutionary shift in how organizations across various sectors manage risk, ensure compliance, and improve performance. The study’s exploration of data analytics in sectors where internal auditing can be enhanced suggests significant benefits and wide-ranging applications for this new approach. Across industries such as finance and banking, healthcare, manufacturing, technology, and government, data analytics has empowered internal audit functions to become more effective, efficient, and aligned with clients’ demands for value-driven services.

In the finance and banking sector, for example, data analytics helps internal auditors validate fraud detection, strengthen risk management, and uphold strict regulatory standards. Similarly, in healthcare, applications such as claims and billing audits, patient data security, and fraud detection are crucial for safeguarding both patient information and financial integrity. In manufacturing and supply chain management, data analytics enhances inventory optimization, improves supply quality control processes, and mitigates supply chain risks, contributing to operational resilience and excellence.

In the technology and IT services sector, data analytics equips internal audit functions with powerful tools to tackle cybersecurity challenges, improve IT governance, and strengthen incident response capabilities, thereby protecting critical assets and infrastructure from evolving cyber threats. The government sector also benefits from data analytics, which enhances financial management, improves program performance, strengthens fraud detection, and ensures public resources are effectively allocated. This level of transparency facilitates accountability and allows services to be subject to citizens' scrutiny.

Across these sectors, data analytics not only identifies risks and weaknesses but also provides solutions for process improvements, cost reduction, and more informed strategic decision-making. This ultimately enhances an organization’s innovativeness and competitiveness. For the successful adoption of data analytics in internal audit functions, a strategic mindset, robust infrastructure, and a learning culture are essential. As organizations continue to operate in a rapidly changing technological landscape, data analytics has become an indispensable tool for ensuring the effectiveness of internal audits, allowing auditors to stay ahead of the curve, innovate, and thrive in the digital age.

By exploring the potential of data analytics, internal audit functions can push the boundaries of what is possible, enhancing risk evaluation and management while becoming trusted sources of value creation within organizations. Furthermore, the integration of blockchain technology further enhances data privacy. Unlike traditional centralized systems, where personal data is stored in a single vulnerable database, blockchain ensures that data from involved parties is encrypted and independent from the network, offering a cost-effective solution for safeguarding personal privacy. Blockchain’s consensus algorithm maintains this privacy, with any new features or developments requiring agreement from existing miners. This democratic approach ensures system stability and enhances transparency, further bolstering trust in the audit process.

Chapter 10

Artificial Intelligence-Based Capital Structure Management:

A Comparative Analysis of Sectoral Dynamics of Leverage

Yunus Emre Akdogan

https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1761-2869

Yozgat Bozok University, Turkey

ABSTRACT

In this study, artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques are used to comparatively analyze financial indicators affecting capital structures in the energy, information technology and machinery sectors. The unique financial structure of each sector leads to differences in capital structure management strategies. Lasso regression, ElasticNet and LightGBM machine learning algorithms were applied to determine the importance of the characteristics for each sector. The analysis reveals that LightGBM has the highest predictive performance when highlighting sector-specific variation in key metrics such as current ratio, asset growth rate and EBITDA margin. The findings underline the importance of AI-based models in financial analysis, which support strategic decision-making by revealing industry-specific priorities and contribute to more effective capital structure management and risk mitigation strategies.

1. INTRODUCTION

Capital structure decisions refer to the way a firm finances its investments by finding the ideal balance between equity and liabilities. In this context, the ideal capital structure maximizes firm value, minimizes financial risk, and reduces control dilution. It continues to be an important area of research in corporate finance due to its profound effects on firm value and risk management. (Jensen & Meckling, 1976; Harris & Raviv, 1990, 1991; Stulz, 1990).

Capital structure is also one of the most important indicators that reveal the risk management strategies of enterprises. Especially for firms operating in different sectors, the structure and impact of debt financing vary in line with the economic, operational, and financial dynamics of the sectors. In this context, determining the factors affecting the capital structure of enterprises operating in different sectors and analyzing the importance of the qualifications are of great importance both in terms of increasing the effectiveness of financial management processes and contributing to the risk assessment processes of investors. (Ahmad et al., 2012; Rehan et al., 2023).

The use of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) methods in financial analysis and decision-making has rapidly increased in recent years, improving strategic decisions across various sectors. (Nguyen et al., 2023; Wall, 2018). In this context, the application of machine learning and artificial intelligence to capital structure theories allows for the consideration of a much larger number of variables compared to traditional regression models and reveals the complex relationships between factors affecting capital structure decisions (Kraus & Litzenberger, 1973). Determining the importance of explanatory variables in capital structure forecasting with machine learning aids firms' financial risk management and strategic decision-making.

This study aims to analyze the factors affecting debt ratios in the energy, IT, and machinery sectors, highlighting their impact on financial leverage. The results provide important insights into how sectors manage financial leverage and reveal how borrowing policies differ across sectors. This will provide investors and financial managers with a guiding perspective to develop financial strategies appropriate to sectoral dynamics. The structure of this chapter is organized as follows. The next section begins with a review of relevant literatures. Section 3 provides a detailed overview of the data used in this study and the methodologies employed to analyze the data. Section 4 evaluates the predictive performance of the models used. Section 5 investigates the importance of various features in the models. Section 6 offers practical solutions and recommendations. Section 7 concludes.

2. REVIEW OF LITERATURES

2.1 Capital Structure Theories

Capital structure theories aim to explain how a firm balances its debt and equity components and how this balance affects the firm's performance. One of the most well-known of these theories Modigliani & Miller (1958) developed by Modigliani-Miller. According to the Modigliani-Miller theorem, capital structure has no effect on the market value of a firm. The value of the firm is solely determined by the risk associated with its profits. However, this theorem is valid in the absence of factors such as taxes, bankruptcy costs, and information asymmetry. In the real world, the presence of these factors causes firms to carefully adjust their level of borrowing and capital structure. Indeed Modigliani & Miller (1963) revised their previous theories and included the effect of tax in the model. In this context, the tax shield theory argues that tax deductible interest expenses provide firms with a tax shield, and therefore, borrowing can increase firm value. In other words, since interest expenses on debt are tax-deductible, firms may increase borrowing to take advantage of this tax shield. However, the theory of bankruptcy costs states that an increase in borrowing increases the firm's risk of bankruptcy, and in this case, borrowing may create excessive costs. When a firm carries a high debt burden, the risk of bankruptcy and the associated costs may reduce the value of the firm. Therefore, firms borrow to the point where the tax benefit of borrowing an extra dollar equals the cost of the increased probability of financial distress (Kraus & Litzenberger, 1973).

Another important theory, the signaling theory, argues that capital structure can provide information about the firm to the outside (Ross, 1977). The level of debt can provide information about a firm's future cash flows and risks. For example, high borrowing can signal to investors that the firm has strong profitability prospects and will be able to repay its debts.

Hierarchy theory, on the other hand, suggests that firms make financing decisions in a hierarchy. According to this theory, due to information asymmetry and adverse selection problems, firms prefer to obtain financing primarily from internal sources and resort to external financing as a last resort. This approach is associated with information asymmetry and the high costs of external financing, especially the costs of issuing equity (Myers, 1984, 2001; Myers & Majluf, 1984). When firms have insufficient internal resources, they first turn to borrowing, with equity issuance being the last preferred method of financing.

In conclusion, capital structure theories play an important role in explaining how firms shape their financing strategies. Each theory offers different perspectives to guide firms in balancing debt and equity and has different effects on firm performance, risk management and market capitalization. Today, new technologies such as machine learning have the potential to make significant contributions to these decision processes.

2.2 Artificial Intelligence and Capital Structure

In recent years, studies on machine learning and capital structure have gone beyond traditional methods in determining capital structure. These approaches aim to optimize financing decisions by using a larger dataset and algorithmic models to determine the optimal capital structure of firms. In this context, the relevant literature is presented below, and previous studies that form the theoretical basis of the current study are reviewed.

Tellez Gaytan et al. (2022) aimed to evaluate the predictive performance of capital structure in financial markets and identify the best forecasting model. They analyzed the capital structure of nine firms with the highest market capitalization operating in Brazil, China, and Saudi Arabia in the Emerging Markets index using artificial neural networks, support vector regression, and linear regression forecasting methods. The study focused on a dataset of 46 observation units consisting of 15 financial ratios taken from quarterly financial statements for the period from Q1 2010 to Q2 2021. The results revealed that ANN models were the most appropriate for nonlinear data, while linear regression models performed better in linear scenarios. The study also found that ANN networks were superior to other models in predicting capital structure, especially in emerging markets.

Eliasy and Przychodzen (2020) investigated whether artificial intelligence could be used in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and whether AI could provide more accurate estimations of expected returns. The cost of capital defines the minimum expected return on any investment made by a firm. Therefore, an accurate estimation of the cost of capital is essential for managers to maximize the value of the firm. To explore this, the study examined the closing prices of the top 10 US-based technology companies listed in the S&P 500 from January 1, 2013, to January 1, 2019. The results showed that the use of artificial intelligence increased the accuracy of the cost of equity capital estimates by more than 60%. The strong ability of the selected deep-learning neural network to predict stock prices improved the accuracy of predicting returns by at least 18%. This study concludes that artificial intelligence has significant potential to replace traditional asset pricing models in the near future.

Bilgin (2023) aimed to select control variables for empirical capital structure studies using nonlinear machine learning methods to minimize variable bias, which is often neglected when identifying potential determinants of leverage. The analysis covered 32,401 firms from 58 countries over 18 years, from 2002 to 2019. Bilgin used the LASSO method to determine the marginal contribution of cash assets, non-debt tax shield, and the current ratio. The results revealed that these indicators are significant factors affecting firms' leverage decisions and should be controlled for in empirical capital structure studies.

Huang et al. (2021) used the decision tree method to analyze the relationship between dynamic capital structure and firm performance. The study examined whether the debt ratio, which companies adjust continuously over time to achieve the optimal capital structure, is a determinant of company performance. They also investigated whether the association rules used in the decision tree method could uncover hidden relationships between variables that contribute to company performance. The study found that companies with low debt ratios perform better, but Tobin's Q and ROA deteriorated as the debt ratio increased. They also found that the speed of adjustment was negatively related to firm performance, suggesting that companies may still perform poorly due to deviations from optimal leverage. Finally, they concluded that not only capital structure but also other variables, such as the price-earnings ratio, research and development expense ratio, and dividend payout ratio, influence firm performance.

Amini et al. (2021) investigated whether machine learning models predict leverage better than linear models by constructing a larger set of leverage determinants, target leverage, and the predictive power of financing actions. They used a large sample of 128,417 firm-year observations from 1972 to 2018 and employed random forest, gradient boosting machines, neural networks, generalized additive models (GAM), and LASSO models for the analysis. The comparative analysis between machine learning and linear models showed that machine learning methods select leverage determinants more comprehensively, provide more accurate target measures, and increase the speed of adjustment by estimating firms' financing models more consistently. The study also allowed for the determination of the relative importance of factors affecting the process of achieving target leverage.

Karlsen and Mathisen (2021) investigated the application of machine learning to predict capital structure and compared these advanced methods with traditional models. They analyzed data from Scandinavian companies, including Finland, from 1990 to 2019. The study found that techniques such as random forest and LASSO outperformed the traditional OLS model by reducing error rates by 5% to 49%, which contributed to faster adjustment of firms to target leverage. They also compared Norwegian and Finnish companies and revealed sectoral differences. As a result, they concluded that a single model cannot accurately predict capital structure and that combining multiple factors and machine learning methods significantly improves the accuracy of forecasts.

Ghosh (2024) analyzed the 2017-2024 financial data of 51 U.S. firms from different sectors, including Technology, Automobile, Food, Manufacturing, and Airlines, using machine learning methods to predict firms' decisions to change their capital structure in the future. In the analysis, more than 600 financial parameters that may affect the capital structure change decision were considered, and the 10 most effective parameters were identified. The study reveals that the random forest method shows very successful results in predicting firms' decisions to change their capital structure in the near future.

Janabi and M (2021) aimed to optimize economic capital structures using machine learning and enhance capital structures, particularly in complex and illiquid markets, by more accurately modeling liquidity and market risks. The analysis results strongly confirm the importance of applying financially and operationally meaningful nonlinear and dynamic constraints in liquidity-adjusted VaR optimization.

Myrland et al. (2022) focused on the leverage decisions of 161 Norwegian shipping companies to examine the determinants of businesses' borrowings using various regression models, including machine learning. The time horizon analyzed covers the period from 2008 to 2019, and they find support for the theory of multiple debt utilization. They also found that tangibility is the variable with the highest impact on the leverage ratio. Additionally, they identified a positive relationship between tangibility and leverage and a negative relationship between profitability and leverage, concluding that the findings support all three capital structure theories.

Qi and Wang (2021) constructed a final sample of 24,512 firm-year observations from 2,541 firms to investigate the frequency and nature of debt structure changes by U.S. firms and to analyze how firms change their debt financing over time using machine learning methods. They also examined differences in debt structure adjustments across firms with different credit ratings and investigated how financial constraints affect the frequency and motivations behind these changes. They found that firms change their debt structure frequently, with more than one-third of firms changing their debt structure every year, and the changes usually last for more than three years. They also found that firms with high credit quality adjust their structure to reduce borrowing costs, while firms with low credit quality change their structure more frequently than firms with high credit quality.

3.2 Methodology

Artificial intelligence and machine learning, with its ability to identify patterns in financial data, provide the ability to analyze a wide range of factors that affect firms' financial performance and risk profiles (Huber, 2019). In other words, compared to traditional regression models, machine learning algorithms have the capacity to take into account a much larger number of variables and have the potential to reveal complex relationships among factors affecting capital structure decisions. (James et al., 2023). However, the most important challenge in research with artificial intelligence is to determine the best method and algorithm for training models. For this reason, in attempts to develop artificial intelligence for any purpose, many algorithms are tried and the most successful method is chosen as the final decision maker. (Ballings et al., 2015). In this study, the determination of the fundamental dynamics of the capital structure is performed with Lasso regression, ElasticNet and LightGBM algorithms and the performance of the algorithms are compared. 80% of the data is used for training and 20% for testing. In the analysis, 5-layer cross-validation was performed. The most suitable parameters for each method and sector were determined by GridSearch method.

3.2.1 Lasso Regression

Lasso regression is a regression method used for variable selection and regularization in high-dimensional data sets. This model minimizes the sum of squares of the error term when determining the regression coefficients and also applies a penalty based on the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients (Tibshirani, 1996). In other words, the Lasso regression method uses the regularization term L1 to reduce the regression coefficients. While this penalty term ensures that the parameters are kept within a certain limit, it causes some coefficients to be exactly zero. Thus, the coefficients of unnecessary variables are reduced to zero and variable selection is done automatically (Emmert-Streib & Dehmer, 2019; Fan & Lv, 2010). In this way, only the most important variables are included in the model, reducing the risk of overfitting and creating simpler, more interpretable models (Emmert-Streib & Dehmer, 2019).

In Equation 1 yi i-th observation value of the dependent variable, xij j-th value of the independent variables at the i-th observation, βj coefficient of the j-th independent variable, λ the regularization parameter or the weight of the penalty term, n number of observations and p represents the number of independent variables. The first part of the model minimizes the error in classical linear regression, while the second part of the model, expressed as the penalty term ($\lambda{\sum_{j = 1}^{p}\left| \beta_{j} \right|}$) makes the model simpler by minimizing the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients (Zhao & Yu, 2006). Some of the penalties applied in the model βj The fact that the coefficients are exactly zero allows Lasso to make variable selection. Thus, unnecessary independent variables are completely removed from the model.

3.2.2 Elastic Net

Elastic Network is a method that combines the advantages of Ridge and Lasso regression. Like Lasso regression, it creates reduced models by assigning zero coefficients. It avoids the problem of overfitting by regularizing the regression coefficients and provides better performance on high-dimensional data. Elastic Net, whose mathematical description is given in Equation 2, uses both L2 norm (Ridge) and L1 norm (Lasso) penalties to select features and deal with multicollinearity issues. In this way, it both ensures that insignificant variables are zeroed out and allows highly correlated variables to be modeled together. Therefore, Elastic Net has the potential to often outperform Lasso, especially for highly correlated estimators.

Where:

The Elastic Nesh is identical to Lasso when α = 1. As α decreases towards 0, the Elastic Nesh approaches the ridge regression. For other values of α, the penalty term Pα(β) interpolates between the L1 norm of β and the squared L2 norm of β.

3.2.3 LightGBM

LightGBM is a boosting algorithm that works quickly and efficiently on large and high-dimensional data sets. It has been developed as an alternative to XGBoost and is particularly advantageous in terms of speed and memory usage. LightGBM is based on gradient boosting, where each new tree corrects errors made by previous ones. At each iteration, the target variable yi the value estimated with ŷi between the previous trees. Therefore, each tree improves by focusing on the errors of the previous trees (Ke et al., 2017).

In the LightGBM model, the objective is to add a new decision tree that minimizes the loss function using negative gradients. Both the L2 norm (MSE) and the L1 norm (MAE) support loss functions.

In Equation 3, d is the splitting criterion, n is the total number of points, j is the feature for which splitting is applied, a is the sampling rate for large gradient data, and b is the sampling rate for small gradient data.

LightGBM uses a leaf-wise strategy, augmenting only the leaf that achieves maximum error reduction, unlike level-wise strategies that expand all leaves simultaneously. This strategy increases the depth of the trees but provides better accuracy and faster optimization (Ke et al., 2017). However, the tendency of the leaf-wise approach to build a deeper decision tree can lead to the problem of overfitting. To overcome this problem, LightGBM imposes a maximum depth constraint in addition to the Leaf-wise method, thereby reducing the risk of overfitting while ensuring efficiency. (Wang et al., 2022). Another aspect of LightGBM that differs from the kasik gradient boosting decision tree is that it uses a histogram to determine the optimal segmentation point. Histogram-based data grouping increases the processing speed by dividing continuous variables into intervals. Another difference of the LightGBM algorithm is that it uses Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) to select samples with large gradients to weight the training. Finally, LightGBM has an Exclusive Feature Bundling approach that reduces the number of dimensions by grouping mutually exclusive features in the same group (Zhang & Gong, 2020).

4. PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE

In the first stage of the analysis, the leverage ratio for each sector is treated as the dependent variable and the other 17 variables listed in Table 1 are treated as independent variables. For each sector in the analysis period, Lasso regression was trained separately with ElasticNet and LightGBM algorithms and four metrics, namely RMSE, MAE, R2 and MAPE, were used to evaluate the forecasting performance of each machine learning model.

The analysis is carried out with three different machine learning methods for each sector for stocks traded on Borsa Istanbul, whose stocks are active in IT, Energy and Machinery sectors. Table 3 shows the forecasting performance of different machine learning methods (Lasso Regression, ElasticNet and LightGBM) in terms of various metrics (RMSE, MAE, R2, MAPE) in three different sectors (IT, Energy and Machinery). The analysis results are evaluated separately for each performance metric.
