RMSE is obtained by taking the square root of the Mean Squared Error (MSE). This metric, defined in Equation 4, makes the magnitude of forecast errors more understandable and expresses them in the same unit. A low RMSE score indicates that the model predicts with high accuracy.

The RMSE values for the IT sector for Lasso Regression and ElasticNet are 27.39 and 27.48, respectively. These values indicate that the predictions of both models in the IT sector have a rather high margin of error. This indicates that the model does not learn complex relationships well enough or that the data show high variance. In the energy sector, the Lasso regression performs better with an RMSE of 20.28, but still above an acceptable margin of error. ElasticNet achieves a better result with a value of 18.99. For the machinery sector, the RMSE of both methods is 7.27, indicating a very low margin of error. This shows that the models are better able to learn the relationships in this sector and the accuracy of their predictions increases. The LightGBM method performs quite well in the IT sector with an RMSE of only 4.13.

Another performance metric is Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Defined in Equation t, MAE is calculated by averaging the absolute values of the forecast errors. This metric evaluates the accuracy of the model's predictions independently of the error values.

For the IT sector, the MAE values for Lasso regression and ElasticNet are 21.00 and 21.02, respectively. For both models, these values indicate that the predictions are not very close to the actual values. In the energy sector, Lasso and ElasticNet perform similarly with MAE values of 15.60 and 14.65 respectively, indicating that Lasso has a larger margin of error than ElasticNet. In the machinery sector, the MAE value is quite low and acceptable with 5.82. Since Lasso and ElasticNet share the same value here, it shows that this sector is predicted with less margin of error than the others. LightGBM has the lowest MAE values (3.12 and 7.12) in both IT and Energy sectors, indicating that this model has a strong forecasting performance regardless of the sector.

In the analysis, the R-square metric is used to measure how much of the variance of the dependent variable is explained by the model. When the R-square defined in Equation 6 is close to 1, it indicates that the variance of the dependent variable is well explained by the model.

In the IT sector, Lasso and ElasticNet each have a low R2 value of 0.14. This shows that the model cannot adequately explain the variance in the dependent variable using the independent variables. In the energy sector, the R2 value of Lasso is 0.22 and ElasticNet is 0.32. Although this shows that the explanatory power of the model is slightly better, it is still at a weak level of explanation. In the machinery sector, the R2 value is quite high at 0.80, indicating that the model is able to capture the relationship between the independent variables and the dependent variable well. The LightGBM model has an excellent explanatory power, especially in the IT sector with a value of 0.98, while it shows a strong fit in the Energy and Machinery sectors with values of 0.83 and 0.92 respectively.

The final metric used to evaluate the results of the analysis is Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). MAPE, defined in Equation 7, shows the accuracy of a model's predictions in percentage terms. It is the average of the ratio of the absolute error between the predicted and actual values to the actual value.

In equationsn number of data points, yi real value, ŷi estimated value and $\overset{-}{y}$ represents the average of the true value.

In the IT sector, Lasso's MAPE value of 144.28 and ElasticNet's MAPE value of 145.04 are quite high, indicating that the predictions of these models are far from reality. In the energy sector, the MAPE value is 45.34 for Lasso and 42.79 for ElasticNet. This shows that both models have an acceptable forecasting success, but there is still room for improvement. In the machinery sector, the MAPE value of 10.59 is a very good result. This shows that the predictions in the machinery sector are close to reality and both models work effectively. LightGBM is quite successful with MAPE values of 12.54 in the IT sector, 19.77 in the Energy sector and 6.30 in the Machinery sector. These results show that LightGBM is able to make very strong predictions in each sector and the MAPE value is quite low.

The results can also be evaluated on the basis of sectors rather than error metrics. Lasso and ElasticNet, the machine learning methods used to explain the dynamics of capital structure in the IT sector, stand out with their high error values. The R2 value of only 0.14 indicates that the model is weak in explaining the variance of the dependent variable. On the other hand, LightCMM shows a remarkable performance by significantly reducing the RMSE and MAE values and increasing the R2 value to 0.98, indicating that the model almost completely explains the variance of the dependent variable. This shows that LightCMM is better able to learn complex relationships in the dataset.

In the analysis for firms in the energy sector, ElasticNet outperforms Lasso in explaining the determinants of capital structure with lower RMSE and MAE values and higher R2 value. LightGBM also performs impressively in this sector with lower RMSE and MAE values and a high explanatory power with an R2 value of 0.83. In the energy sector, all models perform better overall, with LightGBM replacing Lasso and ElasticNet.

In the machinery sector, Lasso and Elastic Net perform equally well in predicting capital structure. Both models have very low error margins with RMSE and MAE values. The R2 value provides a high explanation with 0.80, while the MAPE value is satisfactory with 10.59. LightGBM is also effective here, further reducing the RMSE and MAE values and increasing the R2 value to 0.92, providing a high explanatory power. Overall, while all methods perform well in the Machinery sector, LightGBM stands out with the lowest error rate.

These results reveal that sectors are important factors to be considered in the selection of machine learning models due to their data characteristics and complexity. In other words, the findings reveal that LightGBM is a model that should be preferred, especially by performing effectively on complex data sets and taking into account sectoral differences.

5. FEATURES IMPORTANCE

Determining the importance of features in machine learning models is a critical step to increase the success and explainability of the model. By determining the extent to which each input contributes to the model output, feature importance both optimizes model performance and makes decision-making processes transparent. In other words, analyzing feature importance in machine learning models, which are defined as “black boxes”, helps to understand how the model makes decisions and provides transparency and explainability to the model.

In LightGBM, feature importance can be evaluated with three different metrics (LightGBM - ELI5 0.11.0 documentation, n.d.). One of these metrics is the number of splits. The number of times the model uses a feature in the decision trees indicates that this feature has a high potential to improve the model and is considered more important. The gain metric is calculated according to the degree to which each split reduces the error rate (loss function) or better separates the dataset. Features with greater partition-based gains are considered more important. Cover refers to how much of the dataset is covered by the total number of splits in which a feature is used in the model. It shows how many data samples the feature is effective on. In this study, feature importance was determined by the number of splits.

Figure 1. Feature importance with LightGBM for energy sector

Figure 1 shows the feature importance calculated with LightGBM for the Energy sector. Due to its capital-intensive nature, the energy sector constitutes an important focus on debt utilization and financial leverage in financial strategies. According to the feature importance ranking obtained with the LightGBM model, the main factors affecting the debt ratio in the energy sector can be interpreted as follows.

Considering macroeconomic conditions, the high importance of GDP on the debt ratio indicates that the energy sector is directly affected by economic cycles. This may be due to the increase in energy demand and investments during periods of accelerated economic growth, which in turn leads to an increase in companies' funding needs. Another highly significant ratio is asset growth rates. High asset growth rates imply that companies will need more financing in the future and thus their debt ratios may increase. This is because growth in the energy sector is associated with large infrastructure projects, which are often financed with debt. Another important variable is the EBITDA margin. The high significance of the EBITDA margin indicates that firms' operational profitability is important in sustaining financial leverage. This is because high operating profitability increases debt repayment capacity, allowing firms to have higher debt ratios. The current ratio, which is one of the variables with high significance, indicates the short-term debt repayment capacity. For energy companies, a high current ratio indicates a strong ability to finance short-term debt and better management of debt ratios. Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio, on the other hand, shows the capital efficiency of energy companies through the efficient use of fixed assets. Efficient use of fixed assets may increase the leverage ratio by enabling more debt issuance. The PD/DD ratio, which is one of the market-related ratios, reflects the market perception of the firm. In other words, a high PD/DD ratio reflects investors' confidence in the firm, which may affect the firm's borrowing costs and enable it to utilize leverage more effectively.

This analysis shows that the most important determinants of debt ratios in the energy sector are economic growth, asset growth, operational profitability and capital efficiency. In particular, the impact of macroeconomic indicators such as GDP and asset growth reveals the sector's sensitivity to economic cycles. Moreover, the current ratio and EBITDA margin stand out as critical elements in terms of borrowing capacity and debt repayment ability. Finally, macroeconomic factors such as interest rates and inflation are relatively less influential in the energy sector. This suggests that the sector's borrowing strategies are largely based on firm performance and investment projects.

Figure 2. Feature importance with LightGBM for IT sector

Figure 2 shows the feature importance calculated with LightGBM for the IT sector. It is seen that one of the most important dynamics of the debt ratio for firms operating in the IT sector is the current ratio. The current ratio shows the capacity of companies to meet their short-term liabilities. Since the IT sector is generally known for its low inventory requirements and fast cash flow, high current ratios may not be very common. However, its direct relationship with the debt ratio indicates the extent to which companies adopt equity-based financing strategies rather than short-term borrowing. One of the highly significant dynamics of the IT sector's leverage ratio is the Fixed Assets / Total Assets ratio. In fact, the IT sector is generally dominated by intangible assets such as software, patents and research and development. However, its relationship with companies' debt burden may reflect whether infrastructure investments are financed with debt. In addition, since both the defense industry and the IT sector are intertwined in companies such as ASELS, which is in the IT sector within the scope of this analysis, this may have led to the Fixed Assets / Total Assets ratio being an important variable. The ratio of interest and financing expenses to operating profit indicates a company's ability to cope with its debt burden. Although the IT sector tends to be low-debt, the importance of operational profitability increases when debt is involved. Asset turnover shows how effectively a company utilizes its assets. For IT companies, this metric is important in assessing the effectiveness of existing infrastructure investments and sustainable cash flow. Low asset intensity can reduce the need to borrow for rapid growth strategies. The PD/DD ratio reflects how much investors value a company's equity. Since IT companies are traded at high valuations, they can achieve high market capitalizations with low debt. This ratio also affects the company's borrowing tendencies and investor expectations. Equity Turnover Ratio is related to the amount of revenue generated by the use of equity. Since financing based on equity rather than debt is common in the IT sector, it can be said that equity efficiency plays a critical role in reducing the debt ratio. Another important determinant of the leverage ratio of companies operating in the IT sector is the asset growth rate. Since the IT sector is characterized by rapid growth, a high asset growth rate indicates that the debt ratio may increase. This metric is an important indicator to assess the financing strategies used to sustain growth. EBITDA Margin indicates a company's operational efficiency against its debt burden. It is also one of the important ratios related to leverage for IT companies, as high profitability has the potential to reduce the need for borrowing or facilitate debt management.

As a result, the fact that the variable with the highest impact on the borrowing ratio in the IT sector is the current ratio indicates that the management of short-term liabilities plays an important role in the sector. Moreover, the importance of profitability and growth indicators such as EBITDA Margin and Asset Growth Rate provide important clues on how companies manage their borrowing strategies during the growth process. While the IT sector's low asset intensity and high equity utilization indicate that borrowing is limited, high market valuation indicators, especially PD/DD, suggest that investor expectations may affect borrowing decisions. These findings reveal the importance of balanced planning of equity and debt management while optimizing the financial strategies of companies in the IT sector.

Figure 3. Feature importance with LightGBM for machinery sector

The importance ranking of the characteristics for estimating the debt ratio in the machinery sector reflects the capital-intensive structure, growth dynamics and financial profitability of the sector. The current ratio is one of the ratios that affect the capital structure of enterprises in the machinery sector the most. This situation points to the high level of working capital requirements of enterprises in the machinery sector. Therefore, the current ratio stands out as a key variable in estimating the debt ratio. One of the determinant ratios on the capital structure of enterprises in the machinery sector is the price/earnings ratio. Price/earnings ratio shows the relationship between market capitalization and profitability. High P/E ratios in the machinery sector may indicate that companies need less borrowing in anticipation of growth. Return on Equity (ROE) shows how efficient the company is in its use of equity. It is important to balance debt and equity in the machinery sector. A high ROE indicates that the company is able to grow without borrowing and uses its equity effectively. ROE is a critical indicator for companies that want to keep their debt ratio low. Similarly, equity turnover rate shows how effectively the company uses its equity. In the machinery industry, which is a capital-intensive sector, limiting debt financing and prioritizing the use of equity have a strong impact on the debt ratio when it is common. Since the machinery industry is a sector that requires intensive physical assets, one of the ratios affecting the capital structure is the Fixed Assets / Total Assets ratio. As the share of fixed assets in total assets increases, the need for borrowing may increase. This ratio has a significant impact on companies' financial leverage strategies. Since growth in the machinery sector requires new investments and expansion, it can be observed that firms with high asset growth rates need to borrow more. This variable is important for understanding the relationship between growth and borrowing in the sector. EBITDA margin reflects operating profitability. When operational efficiency is high in the machinery sector, the need for borrowing may decrease. Otherwise, companies may turn to debt financing to maintain profitability.

As a result, liquidity and profitability indicators such as current ratio and ROE have a determining effect on the borrowing ratio in the machinery sector. The capital-intensive structure of the sector makes the Fixed Assets/Total Assets ratio critical in determining borrowing strategies. In addition, growth indicators such as Asset Growth Rate and Sales Growth directly affect companies' borrowing requirements.

6. SOLUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The findings obtained in this study are analyzed from two different perspectives: regarding the algorithms used in the analysis and regarding firms' capital structure decisions.

In this study, Lasso regression, ElasticNet and LightGBM algorithms are used to determine the importance levels of the features affecting the debt ratio. Since the capacity of each algorithm to model financial data, accuracy, and success in feature selection differ, it is important to compare the performance of these methods. The models used in the study are evaluated in terms of their ability to capture linear and non-linear relationships, their capacity to deal with high-dimensional data sets, and their impact on feature selection.

Figure 4. Comparison of forecasting performances by algorithm and sector

Figure 4 compares the success of the algorithms at the sector level according to performance metrics. Lasso regression is a method that is effective in the selection of features and prevents overfitting of models. Thanks to the regularization process, it provides a simpler structure of the model by eliminating unnecessary or unimportant features. However, the success of Lasso regression is higher when the relationship between the dependent and independent variables is linear. In the analysis of complex financial variables such as debt ratio, its inability to capture non-linear relationships well enough can lead to a loss of performance in some cases.

ElasticNet is a hybrid algorithm that combines the advantages of Lasso and Ridge regression. By using both L1 (absolute deviation) and L2 (squared deviation) norms, it offers more flexibility in selecting features. ElasticNet performs particularly well on datasets with highly correlated features. However, its accuracy may be limited due to the complexity of variables and non-linear relationships in data from the energy, IT, and machinery sectors. However, it offers the advantage of examining the effects of multiple factors on capital structure more comprehensively by keeping more features in the model than Lasso.

LightGBM is a decision tree-based machine learning algorithm that can produce fast and effective results on large and high-dimensional data sets. The advantages of LightGBM are its ability to capture non-linear relationships better than other algorithms and its high training speed. In addition, the ability to calculate the importance levels of features makes this algorithm prominent in multifactor analyses such as debt ratio. In terms of determining the importance of different features such as macroeconomic indicators in the energy sector and liquidity management in the IT sector, LightGBM performed better than Lasso and ElasticNet. Accordingly, the use of powerful machine learning algorithms such as LightGBM enables more effective capital structure forecasts and enables the development of customized financial policies across sectors.

Figure 5. Top five most important feature by sector

The results of the analysis can also be used to analyze firms' capital structure decisions. The findings from this analysis, as shown in Figure 5, underline sector-specific financial dynamics and emphasize that effective capital structure management strategies require specific approaches based on the unique characteristics of each sector.

The energy sector is directly affected by macroeconomic growth and therefore GDP stands out as one of the most critical factors in the sector. GDP growth increases energy demand, which has a positive impact on companies' revenues and strengthens their debt repayment capacity. Asset growth rate is an important indicator due to the capital-intensive nature of the sector; this ratio provides a critical reference for financing new investments. EBITDA margin directly contributes to the financial sustainability of companies by reflecting operational efficiency. Although the current ratio is an important indicator in liquidity management, short-term debts are relatively less important in the energy sector as long-term projects and investments are at the forefront. Fixed Assets Turnover Rate is another important indicator that measures the effective utilization of capital-intensive investments. Firms in this sector should develop long-term financing strategies and provide appropriate financing sources for capital-intensive projects. Planning should be made in line with macroeconomic projections and flexible financial strategies should be adopted against changes in energy demand. EBITDA margin should be strengthened by prioritizing technological investments that will increase operational efficiency.

The IT sector attaches great importance to liquidity management due to rapidly changing market dynamics and intense competition. The current ratio stands out as a critical feature in this sector and plays a decisive role in the management of short-term debts. The ratio of fixed assets to total assets (Fixed Assets / Assets) shows the effectiveness of capital investments in the sector, while the EBITDA / Net Financing Expense ratio reflects the impact of companies' operational performance on financing costs. The Asset Turnover Rate reveals how efficiently IT companies utilize their resources, while the PD/DD ratio stands out as an important indicator in terms of managing borrowing risk. Companies operating in the IT sector should develop strategies to maintain short-term liquidity. In addition, companies should increase their rate of return on assets and improve their cost structures.

In the machinery sector, which is characterized by long production cycles and capital-intensive activities, capital structure decisions require a balanced approach between operational efficiency and long-term investments. In other words, firms operating in the machinery sector have to balance liquidity and profitability indicators due to their capital-intensive structure. While the current ratio is crucial for the effective management of working capital, the Price/Earnings (P/E) ratio determines the cost of capital by reflecting investor expectations. Return on equity (ROE) is an important performance indicator that increases the efficiency of investments in the sector and investors' confidence in the company. Equity turnover rate shows the resource utilization efficiency of companies, and the ratio of fixed assets to total assets plays a decisive role in the financing of capital-intensive projects. Firms in this sector should ensure the sustainability of capital-intensive investments by adopting long-term financing strategies, focus on ROE and P/E ratios to increase investor confidence, and aim for high profitability and efficient use of equity. In addition, measures should be taken to enhance operational performance and ensure efficient use of fixed assets.

7. CONCLUSION

In recent years, artificial intelligence and machine learning have been increasingly used in financial analysis. In particular, the determination of feature importance is a process that increases the transparency and predictive power of machine learning models. Feature importance supports financial decisions by revealing which explanatory variables have more influence on a dependent variable such as capital structure. This type of analysis offers the advantage of detecting complex relationships that are difficult to capture with classical regression methods. Modern algorithms such as LightGBM, Lasso regression and ElasticNet allow for the simultaneous evaluation of a large number of variables in financial analysis and the identification of the most important features.

In this study, the determinants of capital structure at the sector level are analyzed with machine learning methods such as Lasso regression, ElasticNet and LightGBM algorithms over a sample of 71 firms operating in the energy, IT and machinery sectors and traded on Borsa Istanbul for the 2019: Q3 - 2024: Q2 period. In the analysis, the performances of machine learning algorithms are compared, and it is revealed that the LightGBM model can make forecasts with the highest accuracy.

Among the factors affecting capital structure, financial indicators such as GDP, current ratio, EBITDA margin, equity turnover rate, and metrics such as asset growth rate reflecting company growth stand out. However, the unique debt management strategies and financial structure of each sector cause the importance of the features to vary across sectors. Therefore, analyzing sector-specific determinants can help companies develop more effective financial strategies by understanding how borrowing policies are shaped by sector-specific dynamics. In this context, the importance levels of the features are determined by the LightGBM model since it provides successful predictions.

The results of the analysis reveal how the borrowing policies of different sectors differ according to sectoral dynamics. The energy sector stands out with its capital-intensive and long-term investment-based structure. Short-term liquidity indicators such as working capital and current ratio are less important in this sector compared to other sectors. Instead, the share of fixed assets in total assets and asset growth rate are more influential on financial leverage. Since borrowing in the energy sector is generally used to finance long-term projects, the impact of macroeconomic variables such as interest rates and inflation on borrowing is limited.

The IT sector attaches great importance to liquidity-based indicators and equity utilization. Measures such as current ratio, equity turnover rate and asset growth rate directly affect borrowing decisions. In addition, the rapid growth potential and flexible structure of the IT sector require investors to be more sensitive to economic indicators. I In the IT sector, inflation is a more significant factor than in the energy and machinery sectors due to its impact on cost structures and profitability.

Due to its capital-intensive structure, the machinery sector focuses on both fixed asset utilization and profitability ratios. In this sector, the balance between equity and debt is of strategic importance, and indicators such as the efficiency of fixed assets and the growth rate of sales play a decisive role.

This analysis reveals that each sector has different financial and operational priorities and that features vary across sectors in predicting capital structure. These feature importance analyses obtained by machine learning methods make an important contribution to the financial strategy formulation process. Identifying industry-specific critical factors allows investors and managers to manage risks more effectively. In addition, this study reveals that the analysis capacity offered by artificial intelligence plays an important role in making sense of financial data and accelerating decision-making processes, and the impact of these technologies on financial management is expected to deepen in the future. This study contributes to the understanding of debt management strategies that differ across sectors and serves as an important guide for the development of sector-specific financial policies with artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques.

AI-Driven Credit Assessment in Banks and Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs) in India:

A Comprehensive Analysis

Shikha Malhotra

https://orcid.org/0009-0002-0930-8493

K. A. Dhanya

https://orcid.org/0009-0007-7388-6518

ABSTRACT

This study examines the application of AI frameworks in real-world scenarios, including regulatory compliance, fraud detection, credit scoring, default prediction, and portfolio management (Moscato et al., 2020). By leveraging AI to gain deeper insights into borrower creditworthiness, financial institutions can enhance decision-making, streamline processes, and foster a more stable financial environment. However, alongside its transformative potential, the implementation of AI presents significant challenges. Ensuring data quality, improving model interpretability, adhering to regulatory compliance, and addressing ethical considerations are crucial to achieving fair and unbiased outcomes. This paper highlights both the opportunities and complexities associated with integrating AI into financial systems, emphasizing the need for balanced and responsible adoption.

1. INTRODUCTION

Following the development of industrial production and computer science in the eighteenth and nineteenth century respectively, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as the third significant technical revolution in economic history (Ernst et al., 2019). Fundamentally, artificial intelligence (AI) is the computer replication of human intelligence processes, including a broad spectrum of problem-solving abilities (Zhang & Lu, 2021). Machine learning (ML) is a prominent subfield in this discipline that enables computers to learn rules on their own from data. The financial services industry is changing as a result of this rapid advancement in AI, ML, and predictive analytics (Mhlanga, 2020). Banks are using these improvements to better analyze client data, which makes loan provisioning more effective. Applications of machine learning and artificial intelligence in banking and other financial Institutions are constantly growing. There is a similar comparable pattern in other sectors of the economy. One of the areas of finance that has developed the fastest over the past few decades is banking risk management, yet there is always a growing demand for more work in this subject.

Credit risk assessment in the banking sector involves the likelihood of default by the borrowers on their loan obligations and thus increasing the risk for the lenders (Behr & Güttler, 2007). It is important to ascertain the likelihood that the borrower will default on their financial obligations in order to assess credit risk. Conventional methods for doing this include reviewing financial records, credit reports, and historical data. These methods have been effective, however there are some problems (Abdou & Pointon, 2011). They rely on static data, to start with. Secondly, they are unable to adjust to shifting economic circumstances.

With the introduction of advanced technology and analytics in the domain of lending, credit risk assessment has evolved significantly. Fintech technologies and alternative data sources are being used by Indian banks more frequently to evaluate the creditworthiness of the prospective borrowers (Tigges et al., 2024). In banks and non-bank financial companies (NBFCs), data-driven risk assessment entails a thorough examination of large datasets to assess borrowers' creditworthiness, financial stability, and possible dangers. While credit scores and past financial data are frequently the foundation of traditional methods, more data elements are used in the modern approach. In addition to financial information, this also incorporates non-traditional data sources like transaction histories, presence and engagement in social media, and even trends that involve correlated behavioral patterns. Credit scoring is greatly impacted by artificial intelligence, which offers a revolutionary method in contrast to conventional approaches. Traditional scoring schemes frequently fail to capture the intricacies and variations of personal financial behaviors (Ashofteh & Bravo, 2021). Conversely, artificial intelligence (AI) is able to analyze large datasets, identify patterns, and produce predictions with a high degree of accuracy. This makes it possible to assess creditworthiness in a more equitable and customized manner (Leal, 2024). In order to detect possible counterparty risks, AI can also analyze non-financial data from sources including documents from various sources like legal documents, from social media and several others. To spot any developments that can negatively affect counterparty' risk profiles, Financial Institutions, for instance, use AI techniques to track news and social media posts about the customers. Credit limit reviews for counterparties whose risk profile has declined may be initiated (Brigo et al., 2013).

By analyzing vast amounts of counterparty data from internal and external sources, such as financial statements, past data about previous payments made, various levels of transactions done in the past, and more, AI-based platforms are able to detect possible credit problems. AI systems, for instance, are capable of quickly and efficiently analyzing counterparties' financial statements at scale to spot any financial warning signs, such as declining key performance metrics, financial ratios, etc.. (Guo & Polak, 2021). They have the ability to automatically identify and highlight patterns related to late regulatory filings, unpaid employee bills, or deteriorating counterparties' working capital positions. Afterwards, this data can be utilized to evaluate counterparties' financial standing and identify default risk.

Further, credit availability is a major factor in economic expansion. But even with strong foundations and strict restrictions, the Indian economy has a severe credit gap. The credit-to-Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ratio, which is very less for India as compared to other developed economies, signifies a striking difference. Due to high operating expenses and challenging underwriting, the current banking infrastructure does not sufficiently serve micro, small, and medium-sized firms (MSME) and other SME borrowers (Esubalew & Raghurama, 2019). As a result, the impact of this gap is particularly severe for these borrowers. This represents the greatest potential impact that artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can have on the granting and making of credit.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) recently announced plans to utilize artificial intelligence (AI) to gain deeper insights into the operations of monitored institutions. This includes employing tools such as cyber key risk indicators, early warning systems, stress testing models, vulnerability assessments, cyber reconnaissance, phishing exercises, and focused assessments of compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and know-your-customer (KYC) regulations, along with advanced data analytics (Doshi & Pillai, 2024).

AI is revolutionizing the banking sector, with machine learning algorithms reshaping traditionally rigid and non-adaptive credit risk assessment techniques. The growing adoption of AI stems from its ability to analyze vast amounts of data, uncovering intricate patterns and connections that traditional methods often miss (Guo & Polak, 2021).

These AI frameworks have been applied in various real-world scenarios, including regulatory compliance, fraud detection, credit scoring, default prediction, and portfolio management (Moscato et al., 2020). By leveraging AI to gain a more comprehensive understanding of borrower creditworthiness, financial institutions can make more informed decisions, streamline processes, and promote a more stable financial environment. However, alongside its vast potential, implementing AI requires addressing critical challenges. Ensuring data quality, model interpretability, regulatory compliance, and adherence to ethical standards is essential to achieve fair and impartial processes.

2. VARIOUS FACETS OF AI USAGE IN CREDIT ASSESSMENT

The potential for AI applications in banking and finance was described in a recent McKinsey research, which showed how the industry may eventually develop to be worth $1 trillion. Leading analysts from Cambridge have also made it clear that massive amounts of data are necessary for the development of AI applications in banking, and institutions already have them safely stored in their arsenal. The banking and financial sectors have adopted AI-driven credit appraisal widely, altering the process by which lenders determine a borrower's creditworthiness and decide whether to extend credit (Agarwal, 2019). According to experts, artificial intelligence (AI) will assist lenders in reaching over 350 million first-time credit applicants and will at least 33% lower loan delinquencies. By enabling quicker error identification in the information and documentation submitted by loan applicants, AI and ML technologies assist banks in rejecting potential defaulters. Reduction of delinquencies is aided by predictive analytics, which is 90% effective in predicting a potential customer's repayment behavior (Source: ICICI)

These days, a lot of conventional banks are using artificial intelligence (AI) to improve customer service and expedite their loan procedures. Eighty percent of banks acknowledge the potential advantages artificial intelligence (AI) can offer the banking sector (Bhattacharya & Sinha, 2022). Banks are able to examine large amounts of data quickly and effectively in order to assess creditworthiness and make lending decisions in real time by employing machine learning algorithms (Garcia & Lee, 2019). One benefit of using AI in lending procedures is that it can reduce bias and improve credit score accuracy. In addition to credit history, algorithms can take into account transaction data and social media activity, giving a more complete picture of an applicant's financial health. On the other hand, bias and the significance of open decision-making are issues.

The following areas define how AI models can be used/are being used in the credit assessment process by the Banks and NBFCs and revolutionize the process.

2.1 Credit Decisioning

When examining the use of AI/ML in credit decisioning, aspects like supervised or unsupervised learning methods come into play. For example, machine learning (ML) allows the visualization of various factors, ranging from certain attributes of loans like misreported ones or bulllet repayment plans, to default trends in certain regions or states income wise (Salah et al., 2019). This type of research is useful in assessing the repayment ability of the individual. Capital Float utilizes AI for marketing, risk assessment, credit decisioning, collections and also works to avert bad loans from happening in the first place. It also uses artificial intelligence to study consumer spending patterns and therefore provides personal wealth management services and lends money through its app, Walnut (Yadav, 2020). Lendingkart employs artificial intelligence (AI) to process ten thousand data points to assess credit, recover debt, mitigate risk of defaults on loans, and intervene before the loans are defaulted.

2.2 Credit Scoring

At present, many analytics start-ups are working to innovate the perfect alternative credit scoring system (Markov et al., 2022). They are aiming at large Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) to enable them to disburse personal loans to people without any traditional credit scores (Bansal, 2024). Shriram Finance, an NBFC in Chennai, is using Disrupting the Credit Scoring System whereby it does personal loans through CreditMantri, which allows for a different kind of credit score. CreditMantri is a credit score digital marketplace that is helping Shriram Finance in the launch of a score builder for the non-conventional credit score.

The Government of India has made financial inclusion a high priority. By utilizing AI to identify those who are not part of the financial system and do not have a credit history, these efforts can be hastened. Fintech businesses may now create credit scores for these people using alternative data sources thanks to artificial intelligence (AI), such as information from mobile phone usage, family history, and spending and earning patterns.

These scores are then used by banks to find and add new clients. Banks can accurately assess a customer's creditworthiness and expedite loan decisions by using AI algorithms that extract insights from a variety of data entries, including the customer's banking transactions, past financial decisions, social media usage, web browser history, and psychometric tests (Lakshminarayana & Deepthi, 2019).

The Fintech business Loan Frame assesses a borrower's creditworthiness by looking at their profile and using AI and ML. Similarly, in order to lower the risk of default, start-ups like Monsoon Credit Techii and Capital Floating employ AI to evaluate the creditworthiness of MSMEs.

2.3 Early Warning Signals

As past events have demonstrated, the lack of strong early warning systems can have disastrous financial consequences. For example, there were hints of impending trouble, like asset devaluation and client migration, which foreshadowed the 2008 collapse of Lehman Brothers, one of the biggest bankruptcy files in American history. These warning indicators were ignored or ignored for too long, which set off a chain reaction that aided in the development of the world financial crisis.

In a similar vein, the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 brought attention to the necessity of keeping a close eye on such threats. The outbreak that started in December 2019 was only a warning sign that gradually became a major global economic problem. The way banks identify and react to early warning signals has changed dramatically with the introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). Large volumes of data can be instantly analyzed by AI-driven systems, which may then spot trends and connections that might point to possible dangers. By improving risk detection's speed and accuracy, these solutions enable banks to act quickly and intelligently.

These illustrations highlight the vital role early warning signals play in early risk identification, enabling institutions to take appropriate action before it's too late. In the standard account, stress signals will be detected and notifications will be sent to the functional personnel. Hence the bank will be able to take necessary remedial measures and prevent erosion thereby mitigating the credit risk with the use of AL models.

Banks have benefited greatly from E-value serve's Insights First EWI system, which helps them monitor credit risk and make wise lending decisions. Through the integration of this system into their current frameworks, banks have enhanced their capacity to identify early warning signals and efficiently handle risks.

2.4 Operational Efficiency

AI technologies assist banks and other financial institutions to cut costs and improve operational processes. The ability of computers to learn such that they can think and work with human information can be referred to as Natural learning process. Readymade solution such technology is capable of sifting through enormous quantities of data within a given time frame and it will help in cutting down costs while increasing efficiency and precision (Locatelli et al., 2022). More than that, AI also assists the banks in the process of preparing several externally focused reports that they have in relation to their customers. As a result, it improves the service and overall experience provided to the customers. Communication policies and accounts reconciling automated functions are made possible by AI and these functions assist banks in understanding the exposure of risk relating to different accounts. There is a trend towards the usage of chat box and robo advisors in order to assist with a client’s finances without them having to visit the bank. Loan applications, processing and disbursement are made easier for applicants because of the AI-driven applications. One moderately advanced and multifaceted product feature in the banks today is the chat box. Most banks have installed chat buttons on their websites to easily identify customer needs, and they analyze each customer’s behavior patterns on the site, once they are installed. They understand the customers’ way of thinking far better and consequently, offer personal attention and point out the best financial solutions for an individual. Consequently, this eliminates the delays associated with banks using emails and other means of communication. The most commonly and widely used either by Bank of America or any other institution is Erica AI chat box. It was launched in 2018, and as of today, the number of engagements has gone beyond 2 billion, and has also served 42 million banks. In India its application has still a lot to be desired since it though potential exists in its use most females in Europe risk using this. Banks are also given feedback on the risk of credit card debt owing to users as well as instructions on how to manage the debt as well as regular system maintenance. Contact Center by SBI has already enabled it to provide better services to the customers.

SBI's customer service has been enhanced further, thanks to the assistance of an AI powered chatbot known as SIA. Even investment decision making gets a boost through AI driven applications that provide comprehensive analysis of market activities. Investment related expenditures on this area Research and development can be lowered owing to optimal development of Ai platforms that gives cause to over buy or over sell particular stocks. The overall functionality of mobile applications in HSBC bank has the integration of AI systems in the Payme application in order to enhance its payment option. Interactive live assistance (ILA) of SBI cards provides the most uptodate assistance on the goods and services offered. AI enabled chatbot ‘EVA’ (electronic virtual assistant) was introduced by HDFC bank and as of now, it has solved more than 2.7 million customer inquiries since launch. ICICI has also introduced a female friendly chatbot and named it iPal. This system has communicated with over 3.1 million users after its introduction.

Currently, HDFC Bank, the biggest private sector bank in India in terms of revenue, has a proof of concept that aims at aiding coders in quicker coding. The bank is also planning to convert LLMs in assessing critical data banks such as statements to give useful information to its relationship management, phone agents and other sales and service personnel.

Technology company Microsoft is collaborating with other projects, including Axis Bank and Aditya Birla Capital, in order to implement processes that utilize GenAI to change the contact centers and increase sales, as well as revise the claims and underwriting management.

2.5 Fraud Detection

In contrast to machine learning, which rejects or approves transactions instantly for fraud detection, Generative AI enables financial institutions to analyze possible fraud. Any activities that encourage noncompliance with existing laws will be flagged by artificial intelligent systems, and appropriate alerts will be dispatched. This would enable the banks to act on the cases of fraud effectively and in a timely manner. Rule-based anti-fraud solutions are making the detection of frauds easier. Therefore, there is no need to physically confirm compliance. Use of AI also warns on excesses by giving the acceptable risk profile in order to prevent too many defaults. GenAI is also used in decision making during times of currency instability, political turmoil or environmental catastrophes. AI has also been employed for preventing such frauds as Data theft, Phishing frauds, Credit card frauds, Biometric attacks, Identity manipulation through for example, fake signatures, and fake ID cards etc.. When it comes to fraud detection, it usually follows such steps as Data analysis, Pattern recognition, Predictive modeling and Anomaly detection.

Setu, a fintech firm under the Pine Labs umbrella, launched Sesame, the first ever large language model (LLM) in India trained particularly for the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) industries, with aid from homegrown firm Sarvam AI that focuses on artificial intelligence research. LLMs are text understanding cognition processes, enhanced AI based computer programs that have been exposed to an extensive range of text and human languages.

Setu’s co-founder Nikhil Kumar observed that this was a moment when the banking and financial services space could be compared to ChatGPT. There are also other different players in the fintech ecosystem like AdvaRisk, a startup focused on detecting financial fraud, which is backed by ICICI Bank and other investors; Velocity, a cash flow-based financing platform founded few years ago and backed by Peter Thiel’s Valar Ventures; and Gnani.ai, another customer service automation focused startup which is in turn supported by Samsung – all of them help banks enhance their primary operations through the use of data.

Losses from online payment fraud increased from an estimated USD 22 billion annually in 2018 to USD 48 billion annually by 2023. Under such circumstances, there will likely be a significant increase in the proactive monitoring and detection of various fraud, money laundering, and malpractice cases by AI, along with real-time prevention. Finding irregular transactions by looking for trends in a person's spending patterns and behavior is one way to do this.

Data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) shows that, in the second quarter of 2025, online financial scams accounted for an astounding 67.8% of all cybercrime complaints. Between 2020 and 2022, the number of fraud cases rose by 31%, concerningly reaching 1.5 lakh cases in 2022. In one of the instances, Hyderabad’s State Bank of India (SBI) branch manager and his accomplices have been arrested in a Rs 175 crore fraud. The scam involved the use of “mule accounts” to divert substantial funds, according to the Cybersecurity Bureau. MuleHunter AI is RBIH’s in-house (Reserve Bank of India Innovation Hub) developed AI/ML model which when deployed in banks, helps detect mule accounts. A mule account is an account created by one person but operated by another person. These accounts are often used for money laundering and tax evasion.

Technology's capacity to interpret trends and constantly adjust to identify novel fraud strategies will enable banks to increase the effectiveness of fraud detection and prevention while drastically reducing expenses.

2.6 Loan Processing and Collection of Proceeds

Over half of first-time borrowers who are seeking loans from financial institutions get declined. This could change with the growth of technology which is the most common in loan evaluation. It is notable that borrower, as well as lend, processes have abused credit scores, reputation systems and endless paperwork over the years but already Artificial Intelligence is revolutionizing the process of Evaluation of Retail applicants for targeted Lending. In the report by National Business Research Institute, together with Narrative Science, it was outlined that about a third of the country’s financial service providers embraced Artificial Intelligence, approximately 32% towards rendering their services better. Even if it was the fintech companies that incorporated artificial intelligence (AI) specifically to enhance their lending capabilities,” traditional banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) have also embraced this technology to cater for the changing consumer demands (Kedar, 2024).

As stated by the specialists, several financial institutions would be able to acquire close to 350 million first-time borrowers, thanks to AI systems, and would be able to reduce loan defaults by at least 33%. This is because markets rely on AI and ML technology which employs information and document verification to quickly identify potential errors in the loan applicant’s information, hence financial institutions can choose to ignore such potential defaulters (Çallı & Coşkun, 2021; Wang & Kim, 2017). Predictive analytics is 90% accurate in forecasting how likely a potential client will redeem the loan advanced to them, thus controlling the levels of insolvency. If banks and NBFCs avail the opportunity to tap into a completely different data set in order to target the ever-growing youth market in India, thus, create new markets and enhanced lending capabilities (Narasimha Raju, 2023). At the same time, easy credit access for millions of households will stimulate spending thereby boosting the economy. A report by the Boston consulting Group estimates that by year 2023, the digital lending or the online loan sector will attain revenues as high as Rs. 10 Lakh Crores, (ICICI Bank Artificial Intelligence in loan assessment).

2.7 Faster and Efficient Documentation Process

Paper documents are usually converted to digital format utilizing a variety of tools and techniques that can be used by hardware and software to automate procedures or workflows. The document can either be scanned and turned into a PDF, or it can be transformed into an electronic version through the use of OCR software, document management systems, or systems for processing documents intelligently. Analyzing a document entail translating a picture into text for computer retrieval. Numerous methods are employed, such as optical mark recognition (OMR), optical character recognition (OCR), optical barcode recognition (OBR), and intelligent character recognition (ICR).

An advanced method for decoding text within photographs is called output character recognition, or OCR. It transforms texts with visuals into easily interpreted characters so computers can choose what to do next. The handwritten amount, account information, and authorizing signature on checks can all be recorded by banks and commercial lending companies using optical character recognition (OCR) technology. Applications for loans include a variety of papers and data. Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies facilitate the efficient extraction of data and information from physical documents. OCR technology allows modern deep machine learning to acquire additional data points for improved processing results and faster data recording and maintenance.

Making sense of the vast amount of documentation required for commercial lending is a challenge. These days, creative AI solutions leverage business machine learning issue mapping to extract the content of these documents, which is much needed for monitoring the loan and borrower's details. Institutes can quickly integrate an AI-powered information processing framework with intelligent document indexing. Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches have made significant contributions to the amazing advancements made in deep learning algorithms and architectures (Khan & Chen, 2018)regulati. Topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and name entity recognition are examples of ground-breaking inventions that have surpassed more conventional techniques. Additionally, NLP plays a big part in automating compliance obligations. These cutting-edge technologies have decreased labor-intensive, manual work and added value for lending companies.

2.8 Other Examples

HSBC is a worldwide banking and financial services corporation that uses AI-powered voice recognition technology for user identification. While on the phone AI systems utilize distinctive speech patterns and characteristics in banking transactions to verify the identities of customers. This secure and useful authentication method reduces the need for more complex security measures like passwords and PINs. These real-world examples show how artificial intelligence is applied in finance and banking. They demonstrate how the banking industry benefits from artificial intelligence (AI) technologies by increasing productivity, accuracy, and customer satisfaction in a number of areas, such as fraud detection, customer service, risk management, investment management, and authentication procedures (Durongkadej et al., 2024).

The Punjab National Bank has established an internal Utilizing a large untapped potential for value creation, the Data Analytics Center will operationalize analytics possibilities in the method and the final product. Using Big Data, AI, and ML models, the bank set out to implement end-to-end solutions in the following areas: (i) product, sales, and customer acquisition; (ii) channel and campaign management; (iii) customer lifetime value; (iv) sentiment analysis for enhancing customer satisfaction; (v) adoption of digital services throughout the customer lifecycle journey; (vi) branch performance management; (vii) operations, customer service and processes; (viii) risk, collections, and compliance; and (ix) fraud detection and prevention.

3. CHALLENGES IN IMPLEMENTATION IN INDIAN BANKING SECTOR AND NBFCS

3.1 Insufficient Data

AI models created on inadequate and scattered data sets will give unreliable results. Flawed data leads to inadequate models and will have far reaching consequences on the outcome. Since Ai models depend on large datasets to identify the pattern and behavior, insufficient data may lead to some noise rather than useful signals. Hence this may lead to unreliable credit assessments. Lack of diverse data also may affect the lending decisions as it does not represent the wide range of demographics or credit behavior. Limited data may also question the validity of the model.

3.2 Lack of Data Standardization

A standard approach is necessary to ensure uniformity, comparison and compliance with regulations. Lack of data standardization may lead to inconsistent methods of credit assessment which may confuse customers, officials and even regulators. Different regions will have different regulatory requirements and without standard procedure, banks may find it difficult to meet the varying legal requirements and may lead to penalties and operational risks. Incompatible data sets may also hinder the process of sharing best practices and insights thereby hindering the effectiveness of credit assessment tools. On other hand, over standardization may also hinder the system. Banks may be reluctant to experiment with new models if they feel like they cannot adhere to existing standards.

3.3 Data Supplement Concerns

If the supplement data is inaccurate, outdated or incomplete, it can degrade the performance of AI models, leading to poor credit assessments. Some integration challenges may also come if incorporating the additional data from some other sources. While integrating the format may be different or varying data structure or inconsistent definitions may hinder the assessment model. Banks must ensure GDPR (general data protection regulation) when sourcing and using additional data. If the supplementary data is biased or unrepresentative it may exacerbate the biases in existing data resulting in unfair lending practices and reputational damage. For smaller banks sourcing supplementary data will be a costly affair and can strain the budgets. Moreover, supplementary data may not be real time data and delay may occur which affects the timely credit decisions. Different stakeholders in the bank may have different opinions regarding the usage of supplementary data which may lead to conflicts if not aligned properly. A proper sourcing strategy should be developed by banks to overcome these challenges. Data drift can also be a factor which affects the authenticity of supplement data sources. Market dynamics may lead to data drift

3.4 Model Selection and Evaluation

There is no universal choice in AI. Different applications like credit assessment, algorithmic rating, personalized suggestions etc. may need different types of models (Ubarhande & Chandani, 2021). The range of AI and ML models can be at times overwhelming. Banks have to choose the right model that balances complexity, interpretability and performance which can be a daunting task (Patel & Brown, 2021). The selected model to be compatible with available data is yet another challenge. Selecting appropriate metrics for model selection is also important. Financial metrics like ROI, cost savings and customer metrics like satisfaction score, engagement rates etc. can be used for model selection (Schlueter et al., 2016). Some complex models may overfit into the data and perform well in tests but poorly in practical applications. The salaries of the chosen model are also important as the data volumes keep on increasing and new credit products are also implemented. Once implemented continuous monitoring is also required

3.5 Training Algorithms

It is not only the data sets which are affecting the training models but also the training algorithms play an important role in the effectiveness of the model. With multiple algorithms available like decision tree, neural networks etc. selecting the most appropriate one for a specific problem will be a challenge (Jain, 2023). The chosen algorithm needs to align with the data sets and business objectives. Most of the algorithms require hyper tuning which is expensive and complex too. Hence require special expertise in this field. Banks may find it a challenge to implement such complex systems due to the lack of proper infrastructure. Hence it will delay the whole process. Training algorithms require extensive data processing like normalization, encoding, handling missing values etc. Certain algorithms cannot be deployed due to the lack of transparency.

3.6 Embedded Bias

AI algorithms can unintentionally perpetuate biases if trained on biased data or if developers inadvertently incorporate their biases. If the AI model is trained on biased data discriminatory outcomes may come in, which will result in disadvantages to certain groups, race or socioeconomic status. Biased models will not be generally accepted by diversified groups. Hence this will affect the stakeholder’s trust. Ethical concerns about fairness and accountability will be created through biased models. Since AI systems learn from historical data, they are more exposed to bias. If we use AI for recruitment in a company, it can be noticed that most of the selected candidates will be male. This disparity comes because historically that company would have recruited more males that females. This happens also in a male dominated society. This is an example of embedded bias. The challenges due to bias in AI can be data bias, Algorithm bias or lack of diversity in AI development which may lead to unfair decision making.

3.7 Explainability and Complexity

Lack of explainability and complexity of AI tools will significantly affect the trust of users, especially related to healthcare and finance. Lack of proper explanation will lead to confusion since users will not be able to understand how AI systems arrived at a certain conclusion. In healthcare, explainable AIs are mainly used to predict the onset of diseases like diabetics, heart disease and different types of cancers. In sensitive financial decisions like credit scoring, fraud detection etc. it is essential to explain the reasons to customers. But many AI models operate as black boxes, making it difficult to understand the reason behind it. This lack of interpretability in AI can hinder trust and raise concerns (2023, Brindha Jeyaraman). The regulatory requirement of transparency is also questioned if the reasons are not well explained to customers. The more complex an AI tool is, the higher the risk of its unpredictability in a real-world banking environment.

3.8 Cybersecurity and Data Privacy

AI driven data in banks is mostly based on sensitive information like customer profile, financial behaviour etc.. Protecting this data from breaches and misuse is important to avoid financial loss. Banks normally take AI service from third party providers and hence that also increases the chance of data leakage. Cyber-attacks like AI driven phishing, deepfake frauds, adaptive malware is also popular (Enyinaya et al., 2024). Moreover, corrupted and manipulated data can be fed to AI solutions, resulting in incorrect decisions. Sometimes the data will be leaked from the side of employees also.

3.9 User Capacity

It can be difficult to express requests or queries in a way that AI can understand: The wide range of consumers who use banking services and their varying degrees of digital literacy exacerbate the issue. A banking or financial service is only effective if the customer's data is meaningful and comprehensible to the AI systems that are using it. At that point, the AI systems are able to identify their inquiries and provide them with an adequate response.

3.10 Multiple Languages

The AI-enabled communication systems that reach the majority of Indians in their first or preferred language would be the most effective, given the plurality of languages in India. This is currently difficult, though, because there is a dearth of machine-readable vernacular language corpora for natural language processing and generating algorithm training. AI that can process and understand local languages currently lags far behind AI that can only function in English or bilingual mode. In order to effectively deliver banking or financial services, an AI-based communication platform must be able to understand spoken language from the user and answer in the same language.

3.11 Trained Labor

Only a tiny number of competent data scientists are accessible in the nation to work on AI due to the lack of experts with the necessary data science abilities. Apart from the dearth of skilled human capital, the current bank workforce lacks familiarity with the newest technologies and software. The financial services sector must collaborate with Indian institutions to produce qualified data scientists and create internal training programs that would enable staff members to successfully apply AI technologies for banking operations. Universities around the world, including those in the US and the UK, are starting to offer undergraduate and master's degrees in fintech in response to the changes that AI is bringing about in the finance sector. An initiative to teach students about cutting-edge banking technologies has been started in India by HDFC Bank in collaboration with engineering and MBA schools.

3.12 Different Enforcement Strategies

Financial organizations using AI solutions have difficulties due to the lack of consistency in enforcement strategies across various nations and regulators. Different enforcement strategies make it challenging for businesses to adopt global standards that work and to assess the risk involved in using AI technologies globally.

3.13 Regulatory and Compliance Challenges

Regarding regulations, the main issues are those of data security and privacy, especially when it comes to following the law (Lee et al., 2023). Banks have to comply with these requirements while maintaining the security and privacy of consumer data. Additionally, there is a lack of a defined regulatory framework designed expressly for AI in banking, which raises concerns about accountability, transparency, and the ethical application of AI (Lee, 2019). Furthermore, it's critical to match AI applications in risk management with the norms and regulations established by regulatory bodies.

Figure 1. Framework for AI-driven Credit Assessment (FACA)

4. CONCLUSION

Figure 1 summarizes the Framework for AI-driven Credit Assessment (FACA) presented in this chapter. The framework illustrates how artificial intelligence is transforming the lending sector by providing a structured approach to automating key processes such as loan origination, servicing, fraud detection, and risk assessment. As depicted, FACA demonstrates how AI-powered systems enhance efficiency by reducing operational inefficiencies, minimizing human error, and enabling precise data-driven decision-making. This framework highlights AI's potential to revolutionize credit assessment, enhancing accuracy, scalability, and compliance while addressing key challenges in the financial sector.

AI is revolutionizing the lending sector by automating loan origination, servicing, and document management processes. In document management, AI automates classification and sorting tasks, significantly reducing the time and effort required compared to manual processes. Additionally, AI is transforming lending by streamlining fraud detection, risk assessment, and loan decision-making, leading to more accurate and efficient outcomes while minimizing the potential for human error (Edunjobi & Odejide, 2024). As technological advancements continue, AI promises even greater efficiency and improved risk management in the lending industry, positioning it as a key driver for the future of loan origination and servicing.

Manual loan application processing and document management face several challenges, including labor-intensive paperwork, manual data entry, and lengthy review procedures. Reliance on paper applications slows the process, causing delays and inefficiencies. Furthermore, manual data entry increases the likelihood of human error, potentially compromising loan accuracy and raising the risk of processing mistakes. Verifying and correcting information adds further complexity, necessitating time-consuming inspections. These inefficiencies result in longer processing times, higher operational costs, and increased chances of errors, creating substantial barriers to effective loan management.

AI-powered solutions offer a more efficient and accurate alternative. By leveraging machine learning and natural language processing, AI can analyze unstructured data to classify and organize documents according to predefined criteria. This approach reduces errors and inconsistencies while saving time. AI systems are also scalable, capable of handling large document volumes effortlessly. By adopting AI-powered document sorting, lenders can improve accuracy, manage unstructured data more effectively, and enhance compliance, ultimately creating more efficient lending processes.

To remain competitive, financial institutions must address the “innovation gap” by embracing disruptive technologies. This requires overcoming hesitation, identifying early adopters, and creating secure environments for testing and development. Robust data governance and safeguards are essential, as regulatory bodies continue to introduce new guidelines. AI represents a paradigm shift in credit risk assessment, enabling faster and more precise evaluations driven by data insights.

The benefits of AI include streamlined processes with reduced manual effort, early detection of potential defaults, enhanced portfolio management, and improved risk mitigation. Proper implementation of AI fosters greater financial stability and sustainability, contributing to a more robust financial ecosystem. Moving forward, human-AI collaboration will be critical to ensure the ethical and transparent use of AI, balancing technological advancements with moral accountability. This synergy will shape the future of credit risk assessment, paving the way for transformative and responsible innovation in the financial sector.

From Chart to Chart:

Analyzing Lyric Content in Music Streaming Charts for Predicting Stock Prices Using LSTM

Chong Guan

https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7827-1498

Singapore University of Social Sciences, Singapore

Yinghui Yu

https://orcid.org/0009-0009-7461-1983
